speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canada Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in this debate on Bill C-79, because we in the New Democratic Party are definitely opposed to the Government's decision to hand more than one billion dollars over to companies that had deposits with both banks, that is, with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, and to do so despite the fact that the deposits were not insured.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of myths that have been spread around in this debate by some of the speakers on the Conservative side. The story is that the Canadian Commercial Bank was a small Western bank, a regional bank, that was helping the average customer out West and was forced into bankruptcy as a result of the National Energy Program.
Mr. Speaker, I have just looked into the growth figures for the assets of this bank, since some of the Conservative Members have pointed out that the bank was forced into bankruptcy as a result of a program launched by the Liberal Government in 1980.
Mr. Speaker, the facts show otherwise. Between 1982 and 1984, the assets of the Canadian Commercial Bank grew from less than $2 billion to about $4.5 billion, thus tripling within a two-and-a-half-year period. This means that most of the bank's obligations, most of its loans were contracted after the Liberal Government's energy program was put into place. So it was the management of the Canadian Commercial Bank that
knowingly made loans on an unsound basis, which have now forced the bank into bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, it is also clear that it was not just a small bank run by well-intentioned businessmen and women. There is a whole history of poor management at the Canadian Commercial Bank. In 1981, the bank decided to expand and diversify, the result being that 45 per cent of its assets would be in the U.S. This is not just a regional bank! It was a bank with dealings across Canada that now decided to purchase the Westland Bank in California and also to make further investments in the United States.
However, instead of investing in other sectors of the American economy, it decided to invest in the energy sector. This meant that all its eggs were in one basket, or just about.
Mr. Speaker, they knew that nearly half of their business would be in the United States. So it was not a regional bank. [English]
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Members who have spoken on this particular subject seemed to think that this was a jolly little western bank, a regional bank and that it should be encouraged because it was making westerners stand proud and giving them a chance to deal with someone locally who would understand the problems of their region.
What the Conservative Members do not say is that while the CCB may have intended to fulfil that role when it first began, it had many other plans as well. They do not talk about the way in which the Chairman, Howard Eaton, took the bank into all kinds of very shaky financial deals. They do not talk about the link with Leonard Rosenberg, the man who at one time sank Crown Trust, Greymac and Seaway Trust in Ontario, who at one point controlled 27 per cent of the share capital of the Canadian Commercial Bank despite the Canadian rules that indicate that a shareholder's holdings should be no more than a maximum of 10 per cent. They do not talk about the fact that in 1983 a cease and desist order was issued on the subsidiary that the CCB had acquired in the United States, the Westland Bank. The cease and desist order made it quite clear that the Westland Bank had made lousy investments, that its accounting practices were wrong, its lending practices were questionable, its costs of doing business and therefore its overheads were too high. Those were the same problems which prevailed with respect to the Canadian Commercial Bank as well.
In its drive to expand at an imprudent pace the Canadian Commercial Bank almost tripled in terms of assets between 1981 and 1984. Its biggest growth, and therefore the biggest increase in obligations which we as taxpayers are now being asked to pay for, was not taken into account before the

National Energy Program was put forward as some Conservative Members have been saying, but came after the National Energy Program was a fact of life. The various taxes imposed by the Liberal Government were a fact of life. The impact that that was going to have, if there was going to be an impact, on drilling, on exploration and on the growth of the oil industry in western Canada was a known quantity when most of the growth of the Canadian Commercial Bank occurred. Therefore it is a myth for members of the Government to claim as they are claiming that it was the NEP that did this poor little bank in.
Incompetence is incompetence whether it takes place in western Canada or whether it takes place in eastern Canada. Mismanagement is mismanagement whether it takes place in western Canada or whether it takes place in eastern Canada. I think that for Conservatives to use this debate as an excuse to vent their frustrations about the National Energy Program is a complete red herring. They should in fact be looking at the factors that brought this Bank down, looking at the incompetence not just of the management of the Canadian Commercial Bank but also the incompetence of the Inspector General of Banks, both under the old Government and the new Government, and the political incompetence which has led us into a commitment made by this Government to bail out depositors in these banks to the tune of something over $1 billion.
The current Bill calls for a payment of $875 million, but that is not all. The Bill does not count the costs that have already been incurred, including the fact that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is in for some $600 million in insured deposits, $280 million for the CCB and $320 million for the Northland Bank. The Bill does not talk about the fact that the Government of Canada and the CDIC already incurred an obligation of some $120 million in the $250-million bail-out that was entered into in March. The Bill does not count the fact that the Bank of Canada has advanced some $1.3 billion to the Canadian Commercial Bank and some $500 million to the Northland Bank through its rescue efforts over the course of the last six months.
Taken all together, we are talking about more than $3 billion, $875 million of which is a direct charge on the Treasury. The money advanced by CDIC will also be a charge in terms of borrowing from the Government of Canada because the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is broke right now and any money it advances has to be borrowed from the Treasury. Back in the spring, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented a Budget which projected that we would reduce the deficit by $2 billion or from some $35 billion to some $33 billion. Now we see that more than half of that has been taken up through this one foolhardy project. I for one say that the deficit of Canada should not be allowed to rise and rise continuously just because we are bailing out big corporations and individuals who put money into these banks when they should have known the risks they were taking.
In addition, the money advanced by the Bank of Canada may well wind up being a charge. We just do not know yet if we will have to pay that charge indirectly.

What we are seeing, Mr. Speaker, is considerable incompetence on the part of the bank and also of the Government, and we can see this as failure on the part of the Government to act responsibly.
Mr. Speaker, let us first talk about the Government's competence. If a company had financial problems and decided to go to ask a bank for a loan, obviously, a banker would say: Show us all your accounts and prove you are capable of repaying the loan and of recovering once your problems have been solved.
Mr. Speaker, I know people who go to a bank, individuals as well as companies and who are not forthright about their problems. They say: I need $5,000 or $5 million, if they really need $10,000 or $10 million, but they do not want to be frank with the bank because it would refuse to help them if they asked for a more substantial amount.
That was the situation at the Canadian Commercial Bank. The director, the president, the entire executive of this bank decided to hide the bank's real position, thinking they might be able to solve their problems. They asked for a bail-out of $255 million, although they themselves knew perfectly well that the kind of situation they were in would require much more.
Mr. Speaker, for a number of years, the Canadian Commercial Bank had a policy of safeguarding some of its loans by making additional ones.

They gave more money to borrowers to allow them to pay their interest payments and keep their loans from going into default. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the bank knew that, and the Bank of Canada . . . the Inspector General of Banks should have known that as well, but instead of asking the kind of questions a bank would have asked, no question were asked at all.
In fact, last May when we debated this matter involving the $255 million, we saw a very curious situation. The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) at that time assured the House that the profits of the Canadian Commercial Bank would rise. I believe I gave some figures with which she agreed. She said that the estimates were that the bank, which had made only $800,000 in 1984 and which was going into a terrible situation with the write-offs in 1985, would nonetheless make $12 million in profit in 1986; $32 million in 1987; $38 million 1989; and $38 million per annum thereafter.
The Minister of State for Finance used to be a respected excutive on Bay Street. She used to work for the Minister of Finance. He, too, was an executive on Bay Street. 1 wonder

what on earth the country would come to if these people were running the financial affairs of the private sector. Last spring, they were acting as if they were babes in the woods. They were accepting stories which no one in their right mind would have accepted.
Certainly, in participating in that debate, I for one cast my doubts on those estimates of the types of profits which were said to be available. As I indicated, if that type of profitability were available in the banking sector and if the laws of free enterprise worked, then there would be a great many other people to skim off those profits and bring them down to a level which would be more reasonable. In fact, that prediction came true. The bank was nowhere near restoring solvency and nothing was done by the Government to establish exactly what the situation was for a full four months after the Canadian Commercial Bank came in and asked for assistance.
On behalf of my Party I asked where the devil the Bank of Canada was when the press reports came out about the Westland Bank and its problems. I asked where the devil the Inspector General of Banks was. Even if he had only eight inspectors, it seems to me he could well have gone to the tenth largest bank in the country and placed some inspectors in it in order to find out what the devil was going on. If he was not aware of what the situation was, then he was incompetent. If he was aware and was not telling the Minister, then he was irresponsible. Either way, we feel very strongly that his resignation is one of the things which should result from this particular affair.
I am talking not of events which occurred in the course of a month or two, as happened with the rape of Crown Trust in Ontario. I am talking about events which went on for a very long period of time. The rotten management and the rotten management practices at the Canadian Commercial Bank were known for a long time. They were common parlance in the banking industry. The bankers themselves in the big five banks knew the problems they were having with prudent lending practices, in terms of losses which they were taking in Alberta and in British Columbia. They knew, too, that the Canadian Commercial Bank, as a junior bank, was taking risks which they were not prepared to take. Let us face it, pigs do not fly and rotten loans do not turn to gold. Therefore, they knew that the losses experienced by those banks must be a lot greater than the loss experiences they were having with their rather more prudent lending.
Did the Inspector General go in? No. Did the Inspector General hire consultants if he was unable to send his own inspectors in? No. Did the Minister of State for Finance, who must have been seized of these problems when she took over responsibility for the banks back in the fall of 1984, tell him that something should be done? No. The Minister of State for Finance keeps on joking that women are not good enough to sit on the boards of directors of Canadian banks; but now she is running them. Is that not a turn-around? Yes, it is. Quite frankly, I say to her that her responsibility is to prove the type of confidence women can have in the banking sector and not just demonstrate incompetence. We are looking at $1 billion

which will flow down the drain because of incompetence, not just of the staff but of the ministry.
I am reminded of the fact that the Minister said she tried to get a director and could not obtain one. She could have named the Inspector General to the board of directors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and told the management of that bank that she would take him off as soon as they put someone decent on the board. She could have placed officials from the Department of Finance on the board, or even retired bankers, as her nominies. She would have been entitled to do that as a condition of the bail-out. However, that did not take place.
Some three years ago, we saw an example of responsibility under the parliamentary system in Great Britain. The Minister and Hon. Members will recall that at that time the Foreign Office staff in Buenos Aires failed to notify their superiors in Whitehall that Argentina was on the verge of making an attack on the Falklands. The gossip was abroad in Buenos Aires at that time and either the Foreign Office staff, the diplomatic staff, did not know, in which case they were incompetent, or they knew and did not tell Whitehall, in which case they were irresponsible. Lord Carrington, who was a very trusted and very senior member of the British Cabinet, submitted his resignation which was accepted because he took full responsibility for the incompetence or irresponsibility of the people who worked under him. He had no knowledge of this, it was not his fault, but he took the responsibility.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time we had that kind of behaviour in this House of Commons. I suggest that when it became clear to the Minister of State for Finance that the bail-out was not working and that the commitments she, the Minister of Finance, the Governor of the Bank and the Inspector General of Banks made might cost the taxpayers a large amount of money, she should in fact have submitted her resignation-which should have been accepted-because that would have been the honourable thing to do. In this case, as well, I would point out, it is not just a matter of things which were done on behalf of the Minister of State for Finance without her knowing. This was a dosier which was a major responsibility in which she was very closely involved and, therefore, she had the ability to know what was going on.
When the Inspector General did not go in, Mr. Speaker, for months upon months to find out about the other portfolio, the Minister of State for Finance should have demanded his head. She should have said, "go in there and find out what is happening". But she did not. She waited for four months, and that was totally irresponsible.

I would like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by suggesting what we could do with $1 billion. We are going to be told over the next three years that we cannot do all of these things because of the deficit. We are going to be told, "We do not have any money". We have heard that already. The National Research Council is devastated because of spending cuts. Environmental services are devastated because of spending cuts. That is something we could do right now but we will not be able to do it because the Minister of State for Finance blew $1 billion on the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank.
We could spend $150 million as a down payment in developing a national universal daycare system so that women and families could have that kind of care for their kids, which is essential for young families in these days. The Progressive Conservatives promised a nationwide network of transition houses. That was one of the promises made on television by the now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). We could take $50 million and use that to produce 4,000 new jobs for women and support 300 transition houses to provide refuge for women whose lives and health have been threatened by sexual and physical violence, one of whom in Ottawa, in my riding, was killed a few months ago after 30 years of abuse by her husband.
We could use funding to put $200 million into reforestation and put the economy in western Canada, particularly British Columbia, back on its feet. The forests are being raped right now, Mr. Speaker. We could use $100 million to provide farm mortgage refinancing and $7 million to restore Canagrex as an international marketing agency for farmers, again to help the economy of western Canada.
But if our Party proposes these things, the Government is going to say, "No, we cannot do that because we blew $1 billion on Barbara's folly," and that, Mr. Speaker, is inexcusable. That is why we are opposing this particular Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There being no questions or comments, we shall resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-79. 1 feel it is important that we develop the history leading up to the need to bring this Bill forward, what actually took place. I believe this has a bearing on why this Bill is here today.
We were seven months old as a Government, Mr. Speaker, when we were faced with this situation in western Canada. I might point out that these problems occurred far before we, as a government, had the responsibility to deal with this matter. In 1980, changes to the Bank Act resulted in 58 new banks being established in our country. Yet the regulations affecting banks have not even been revised since that date. There has been no regulatory change at all. Not only that, the Liberal Government of the day came out with its famous National
Energy Program which devastated the banks in western Canada. We know the effect it had on our economy, yet the Government made no effort to change the regulations or assist in the development of a regional bank in western Canada. I might add that the NDP supported the Liberal Government in establishing the NEP. As a member of the Government from western Canada, I am very proud that we tried to save these regional banks in western Canada. Regional banks are very, very important to our economy, not only in western Canada but in all areas of the country. Regional banks have the pulse of the community in which they operate. They know the small business community, they are part of it. I am a member of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and we had a long series of hearings during which we had the good fortune to hear a presentation from a well-known U.S. economist by the name of Thibaut de Saint Phalle. He is well known in the economic field. I want to quote the following from page 8 of his brief to the committee:

Regional development is particularly important to Canada given the extent of its undeveloped wealth. It should be high on the Government's priority list. But regional development in no way depends upon local regulatory authority.
He believes the regional banking system is important to our economy, and I support 100 per cent the efforts of our Government to retain these regional banks in western Canada. He went on to say:
Recent events in western Canada involving the difficulties of two small Canadian banks may well discourage the Canadian Government from taking action at the present time on the proposals before this committee. There is always a natural tendency to believe in such situations that the event would not have occurred if there had been more Government regulation. We are passing through a similar phase in the United States during a period of time where savings and loans, a large money-centre bank, and numerous government-securities firms have gone under. If local development, which is so necessary in a developing, though mature, economy like Canada's, is to progress, local banking institutions are in my view to be encouraged regardless of temporary set backs.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to comment on the Opposition's position and the effect it had on this entire situation. Back in March the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Inspector General of Banks, six of the Schedule A banks, along with the Provinces of Alberta and B.C. as well as the federal Government, sat down and decided it was worth while saving these regional banks based on the information they had at that time. That to me was a visible assurance to the people who had money deposited in these banks. This group of Government and industry representatives came together and said that this cash infusion should result in the stability of the bank. That was a visual insurance to the investors and depositors that it was safe to leave their money there. There is no doubt in my mind that the depositors felt assured that everything was going to be fine.
[DOT]	(1130)
What was the Opposition's position on this, Mr. Speaker? It had an integral part in this scenario, and I believe it was a discredited part. There were wild statements made in the House of Commons by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). To give you an idea of how the Opposition was trying

to disturb the stability of the depositors and investors, I would like to quote the Leader of the Opposition as reported in Hansard of September 17. He said:
Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister have authorized the bail-out if he had known, as we now know, that between the time the CCB received a cease and desist order from the Federal Reserve Bank in San Francisco and the time it came before the Inspector General of Banks on March 14, it had transferred all of its good assets and good loans down to the California subsidiary? The California subsidiary is still prospering; it is the Canadian parent in western Canada which is now bankrupt.
A headline the next norning read, "CCB transferred millions of dollars to the U.S., Liberals charge". 1 quote from The Globe and Mail of September 18 the following:
The Liberals charged in the House of Commons yesterday that the Canadian Commercial Bank transferred up to $300 million in good loans to its ailing U.S. subsidiary shortly before the CCB itself received a $255 million bail-out.
The next day in The Citizen a headline read, "U.S. contradicts Grits on CCB cash transfer". The article reads in part as follows:
However, David Scott, deputy superintendent of the State Banking Department in Los Angeles, told The Citizen Wednesday the U.S. Federal Reserve Board did not warn the CCB of a pending "cease and desist order" about Feb. 21 as Turner claimed.
He also said there was no flow of $300 million in assets to the Commercial Center Bank, the CCB's California subsidiary.
I think that was part of discouraging the depositors and investors in the Canadian Commercial Bank. It obviously concerned them when the Leader of the Opposition made false charges of this nature right in the House. This is the kind of support that the Official Opposition gave to the attempt to save a western regional bank. The NDP itself is not without fault. It called for an emergency debate on the Northland Bank.
The Speaker agreed with it and so did you.

They talked about the CCB and its potential failure. They talked about the crisis in the banking industry. All of these words are cause for alarm for depositors and investors in those banks. At that time the Government was trying to assist the integration of moneys into the Northland Bank to help it survive the situation it was in. Therefore, the NDP is not without fault in my opinion. They discouraged the attempted salvation of these two regional banks in western Canada.
I feel that the Government has a moral obligation to help the depositors and investors who stayed with the bank upon receiving visual assurance in March when the banking community got together with the provincial and federal Governments to save these institutions. Who are these depositors?
The Bank of America.

It is interesting to note who they are. If we had decided not to help these uninsured depositors I wonder whether the Opposition would have taken the reverse approach and asked us why we were not helping the credit unions. There is approximately $130 million on deposit by the credit unions and their centrals in these facilities. Does the Hon. Member

for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) have a credit union in his riding which has moneys in that bank?
Three of them.
Is there a school in his riding which is a depositor in that bank?
No.
They are very selective in the way in which they would like this assistance to flow. Among the depositors are pension funds, both public and private, with third parties involved.
Which ones are they?

Why should they not get their money back if there is a moral obligation? Does the Opposition want to become selective and give the money only to the credit unions, universities, colleges, and schools?
That's right.

If it does not want to give any money back, why does it persist in giving the Government heck with regard to transfer payments to the provinces? The transfer payments which the federal Government gives to the provinces cover education, medicare, and the costs of the provincial Governments themselves which have deposits in these banks. On one hand opposition Members say that we are not giving enough in provincial transfer payments, and on the other hand they are criticizing us for helping out the facilities and institutions which happen to have deposits in this bank. I have great difficulty in understanding why, on the one hand they want to save the credit unions but, on the other hand, they criticize us for assisting them in this particular situation. My understanding is that the credit unions have more money invested in these two banks than the foreign banks have. Can we decide to give money only to the credit unions? There are labour unions with money on deposit. Do we give money only to them?
Name them. Who are they?

I find it difficult to understand how the members of the Liberal Opposition can say that $100 million is needed for Domtar in Quebec, and, on the other hand, they criticize the federal Government for trying to help small industries across Canada which have moneys on deposit in this bank. As Hon. Members know, small businesses could have been using this bank as a clearing house. At the time when the bank was closed down they may have had accounts in a surplus situation. They owe people money, and all of a sudden they lost $140,000. This is a situation through which we can help a wide range of institutions by supporting the uninsured depositors.
I would like to refer again to the Opposition's approach to what I call selective aid. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) said that we could assist other agencies with that money. A member of the Liberal Party stood up and said

that the fishermen need $6 million or $8 million in aid. A member of the NDP stood up and said that we must help the farmers. I agree that we have problems in western Canada, but do we become so selective that we decide to help the farmers, but not those farmers who have retired and have their pension money in these banks? Does the Opposition want selective aid? Does it want to discriminate against depositors? Does it feel that there is no moral obligation to those who had faith and tried to keep this western regional bank going?
Not the Bank of America.

Is that the position the NDP has taken? In my opinion we have a responsibility to ensure that our economy continues to grow.
Finally, the statement we hear about a billion dollar bail-out is incorrect.
It is $3 billion.

A $3 billion bail-out is also incorrect. You are assuming that there is a 100 per cent loss on all of the assets of those two failed banks. However, there will be some money left when these banks are wound down. Perhaps it will be 60 cents or 70 cents on the dollar.
It could be 30 cents.

It could be 50 cents or 60 cents. However, we are looking at the difference. For example, if there is $530 million in uninsured deposits, we are talking about only $160 million if there is a return of 70 cents on the dollar. Is it not worth-while for the economy of Canada to spend $160 million on that one bank, if that is the liquidation cost, to save the credit unions, the hospitals, institutions, schools, unions and those third-party depositors who have their money invested in pension plans? The statements in the press reflect a 100 per cent loss, yet we know that this will not happen.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre suggested that all the money will come under general budgetary costs. That is not correct. Members of the Finance Committee know and Members of the House should know that the deposit insurance fund, which is financed by the banking institution, will bear a major portion of the costs. They know that there is a proposal being considered to increase the premium from one-thirtieth of 1 per cent to one-tenth of 1 per cent of the deposits. Yet, Members of the Opposition will not say so. They claim that the taxpayers will bear all the costs.
I am pleased to support this Bill. I believe that we are correct in recognizing the moral obligation to these depositors and that it will be good for the country in the long run. When Canadians realize that the actual costs are much lower than those being projected by the media and the Opposition, they will see that in the long run this measure will be good for Canada and Canadians.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand that I will be the next speaker for the Official Opposition. However, before entering the debate, I want to ask the Hon. Member how he can claim that statements made by the Leader of the Official Opposition on September 17 harmed the confidence of depositors and investors in the Canadian Commercial Bank when the Government itself closed down that bank two weeks before?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that it was harmful to the Northland Bank and the whole banking system in western Canada. It caused fear not only among depositors but among investors about the stability of the banks and whether there would be a run on the banks. The general public does not really differentiate between the CCB and the Northland Bank. They consider it in terms of a western regional bank.
It was not only that statement that was harmful but also the general questioning throughout the period after the infusion of funds took place in March. I believe that the constant questioning on this issue undermined the confidence of those people who may have either deposited or invested in the CCB. I was using the statement referred to by the Hon. Member as an example of how the Opposition would make any statement in order to gain political points. I believe that affected the ability of Northland to find investors to keep it going.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely the lack of confidence in the Northland Bank was created by the Government itself when it linked the Northland Bank with the Canadian Commercial Bank by trying to wind it up last March at the same time it applied to wind up the Canadian Commercial Bank. If the Government itself made that expression of lack of confidence, how can the Hon. Member expect the financial community itself to have any more confidence in that bank?
Furthermore, is it not a fact that doubts about the viability of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank were expressed from the time of the rescue in March and afterwards by financial journalists and the financial community itself, which is well before questions were raised last September when the Government announced that it was closing down the Canadian Commercial Bank? Is the Hon. Member telling the financial community that it should have shut up and not asked any questions?
No, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I have a very short question and, depending on the answer, a quick supplementary. Does the Hon. Member believe in free enterprise? A yes or no answer would be adequate.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I believe in free enterprise.
I also believe that there are moral obligations involved when the free enterprise system is encouraged to save a facility. The provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, the Government of Canada, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Inspector General of Banks and six major banks indicated at the time
October 8, 1985

they invested their money that, based upon the information they had the bank was sound and could continue operations. They asked free enterprise to stick with the bank, and I believe there is a moral obligation to those people who stayed with it pursuant to the assurances they had in March. I believe in free enterprise.

How can this be called free enterprise when there is such massive government interference amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars? It was always my understanding that the free enterprise system meant letting the market forces determine the weak from the strong so that those who cannot compete in the market-place would unfortunately fail. That is what I have been told by many free enterprisers over the years, "If you cannot survive in the market-place, you probably should not be there because you are inefficient".
How can the Hon. Member be a free enterpriser on the one hand while, on the other hand, justify such massive Government intervention and bail-outs? That is not free enterprise at all.

Mr. Speaker, let me throw the question back to the Hon. Member. If he is for free enterprise, does he support the request for aid to the farming community because of the drought situation or do we just let the market-place take its toll? In the case of a drought, it was an act of God, while in the other case it was an act of the Liberal Party with its National Energy Program.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to the National Energy Program and how it negatively affected western Canada. Would he elaborate on that statement, because it would be very enlightening for Members from the east to know how that program affected confidence in western Canada and ultimately how confidence in those banks may have been diminished because of that program?

I thank my colleague for that question. I will attempt to keep my answer short but I could go on for 25 minutes on this subject.
The first impact after the National Energy Program was announced was an exodus of drilling rigs to the United States. Without the search for oil and gas, primarily in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the demand for manpower began to decrease. There was no drilling or construction of new refineries. The demand in the real estate markets for such things as housing and the activity in the business community fell.
These banks obviously had real estate holdings in the various spinoff industries from the oil finds. That was the general impact that took place and one of the major reasons that these banks failed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) moved the following amendment:
this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds.
In speaking about this Bill, and in particular about the amendment, the first point which has to be made is that this Conservative Government must bear the full and ultimate responsibility and blame for a fiasco which will cost taxpayers, not simply the $875 million requested in the Bill, but close to $3 billion in total. I am talking about the Government's bungling first last March of the rescue of the Canadian Commercial Bank, the failure and closing of that bank itself and then the failure of the Northland Bank over the past few weeks. The $875 million, which the Bill indicates would be needed to reimburse uninsured depositors in the Canadian Commercial Bank and in the Northland Bank, is only one part, the smallest part, of what Canadians will have to pay for the Government's mismanagement of the CCB and the Northland Bank affairs. The Government will have to find close to $2 billion to cover the advances of the Bank of Canada to the two banks in question. We are talking about amounts which are very large. Certainly the $875 million in this Bill alone is a very large amount by anyone's standards, by the standards of any Canadian in any walk of life.
There is a basic principle which in this case above all has to apply, that is, if taxpayers' moneys are to be spent, then Parliament on behalf of taxpayers should know who will get that money. If, as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) said, this principle applies to cases such as the travel expenditures of the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Greni-er), surely it must apply when we are talking about billions of dollars, not just thousands of dollars, which have to come from the ordinary taxpayer, the ordinary Canadian.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) said yesterday that the privacy of individuals has to be protected, that was what the law indicated and that was what individual depositors were entitled to, if they were to have faith in our banking system. Surely what she said applies only in circumstances where depositors deal with their banks in the ordinary way and when their banks are doing business in the ordinary way. However, when we are talking about the failure of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, surely we are not dealing with normal circumstances. These banks have failed, and the normal course of action under the law is
October 8, 1985
that depositors would be compensated only for deposits under $60,000. Surely depositors knew that, or should have known that, when they put their money into those two banks. Canadians are entitled to ask why Parliament should treat these depositors differently when it comes to reimbursing them for amounts above $60,000, if these people are not even willing to disclose their identity and the Government is not even insisting that they disclose their identity to Parliament and to Canadians generally.
The Government in itself and by itself supplies the reason for the approach in this Bill. It provides the answer to the basic question as to why depositors should be reimbursed for deposits in the Canadian Commercial Bank and in the Northland Bank in excess of the amounts insured under the ordinary law. The answer is a simple one. The Government is saying that this should be done because this incompetent Conservative Government induced depositors to stay with these banks when it said that they were viable and would survive. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance said over and over again that the bail-out or the rescue last March of the Canadian Commercial Bank made the bank viable. In effect, the Government gave its word that the Canadian Commercial Bank would survive.
The Government was wrong. It bungled the bail-out. It bungled its obligation to monitor the situation properly after the bail-out had been approved by Parliament. This incompetent Conservative Government is asking Parliament, and therefore ordinary taxpayers, individual Canadians, to pay for its own incompetence and its own mishandling of this bank fiasco.
Mr. Speaker, these are extraordinary circumstances and surely the Government's argument that the privacy of depositors should be respected cannot apply in these extraordinary circumstances. The Government says that the Bank Act prevents it from releasing the names of the depositors. I say, show us exactly where in The Bank Act it says that this cannot be done. If there are legal opinions that the Bank Act says this, show us the legal opinions in question; table them in the House. Even if the Bank Act does say that the confidentiality and the identity of depositors has to be respected, surely the Act can be amended to clear up this point to take into account the very extraordinary circumstances that we are dealing with now, circumstances that the Bank Act was not intended to deal with in the ordinary course of its application to the banking industry of this country.
Let me say again, surely the Bank Act and what it says about the privacy of depositors applies only in a normal bank situation where a bank continues to do business in the ordinary way. Here we are dealing with the winding up of a bank, in effect a bankruptcy proceeding, in effect the bankruptcy of a bank. In a bankruptcy proceeding if a creditor wants to be paid what he is owed by the bankrupt firm, that creditor has to file a claim and his identity is public, it is known, it is listed. That list is public. If he does not want to do that, then that creditor's claim is not paid.
October 8, 1985

The Government has failed to provide any convincing and reasonable explanation that any ordinary Canadian would accept as to why things should be different when it comes to paying the uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. I say that no bona fide depositor would feel that the terms on which he or she put money into the Canadian Commercial Bank or the Northland Bank were not being followed if it was a requirement of the law that in order to be reimbursed for uninsured deposits his or her identity had to be disclosed. Those terms were only that deposits were confidential in the ordinary course of banking business and if the bank failed each depositor would get only $60,000 from the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Any person who wants his identity to remain confidential, if that person is a depositor in the Canadian Commercial Bank or the Northland Bank, is saying in effect that reimbursement should be made only for the first $60,000 of the deposit.
In this Bill the Government has gone partway toward the Liberal position in that the Bill says that a depositor must file a claim for the uninsured amount of his deposit. However, the Bill does not specifically say that the depositor's identity must be publicly disclosed. We say that the Government can and should insist on this as a condition of the claim being paid, and in fact the list of claimants has to be made public and this has to be written clearly into the law.
Why should any bona fide depositor object to this? What has any depositor got to hide, or, a much better question, what does this incompetent and bungling Government have to hide? Are we talking about firms or individuals who are particular friends of the Government? What exactly, under the circumstances, is the Government trying to keep back if identities are not disclosed? If the indentities of uninsured depositors are not disclosed, then the Government itself has created doubt and a suspicion which will be left hanging over this fiasco for a long time to come.
We are not talking, after all, only about little guys looking for a safe place in which to put their life savings. The figures tabled yesterday by the Minister also suggest that there are a lot of depositors who put their money into these banks as an investment to get a higher return. A higher return implies a higher risk, and this Government has not yet made a convincing case as to why people who put money in deposits into the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank as investment should not bear all or part of that risk above $60,000 rather than having the burden assumed by the ordinary Canadian taxpayer.
The only real answer to this kind of question is that the Government is saying that the depositors in these banks should not have to suffer from the bungling of the Governemnt and its Ministers and that the burden should be placed on the ordinary taxpayer. There was bungling here, there was incompetence, there was mismanagement of the situation by the Government and its Ministers in how they dealt with this bank fiasco.
The Government is trying to evade its responsibility by talking about the economy of western Canada and by suggest-

We worked out a package", they said, "and it is the right package. We worked it out in consultation with the banks and the provincial Governments. speechtext:

October 8, 1985

I learned the rudiments of finance on St. James Street, which may or may not be in the same league as Bay Street, but the Hon. Member can always consult his colleague, the little guy from Bay Street, and find out whether the principles are different. We were told there is no common link between the depositors and the shareholders of a banking institution. There are some countries where confidentiality is a commercial commodity-Switzerland to name one. We are not prepared to go that far, but had Liberal Party Members attended all sittings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs they would have seen for themselves the banks, credit unions and caisses populaires were all strongly against publishing the names of depositors before or after the collapse of a banking institution.

Member from New Brunswick mentioned it a few minutes ago-that it is the incompetence of the Liberal Government with its National Energy Program which caused this

country so many problems. I do not disagree with that. Last September 4, of course, the voters of this country punished the Liberal Party and threw it out. We are told, Mr. Speaker, to vote for a Bill to provide around $1 billion to the depositors of these particular banks. I represent 70,000 people in the Yorkton-Melville constituency. According to the profile of the Canadian Commercial Bank as of June 30-and I want to put this on the record-the Government of Canada had $14.4 million on deposit; the various provinces had $45 million on deposit; the individuals, and we do not know who all those individual Canadians are, had $308.5 million on deposit. I said, "Canadians". They are not all Canadians, of course, they could be individuals anywhere in the world. The banks themselves had $267.2 million on deposit. Then there is a category called "others". I do not know who the "others" might be. Perhaps they are the Edmonton Eskimo football team, but $774.6 million was on deposit from "others" in the Canadian Commercial Bank. That totals up to $1.4 billion.
I am not about to agree, Mr. Speaker, and facilitate the passage of a Bill which in effect asks Parliament to sign a blank cheque for money which I believe could be used in a much better way. It could be used to create jobs, to help the small business people and, in particular, the farmers of western Canada through an emergency drought relief fund because of the natural disasters with which they are faced. There was a drought in the beginning and now there is snow. That is a double disaster the farmers are facing in western Canada. I believe we can stimulate the economy of this country by helping the base industry such as the farmers and the fishermen. You do not stimulate the economy of this country by helping the big banks.
Mr. Speaker, we now have a Government which is bent on helping multinational corporations as well as the rich in this
country. It is not at all bent on helping the farm producers of Western Canada, our unemployed and ordinary Canadians. [English]
I plead with my friends in the Conservative backbenches to be consistent with their philosophy of free enterprise. Here are two companies which failed because of bad management. If you believe in free enterprise, then the efficient company, the one that can make it in the market-place, will survive and the others will fall by the wayside. Here are two giants who have fallen. I ask my friends in the Conservative Party, why the rush to support a Minister of Finance and a Minister of State for Finance in bailing out these big, big people in our country when they cannot give similar aid or even half of it to the ordinary farmers of the West and the ordinary working people of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I look through the list of those who deposited money in both these banks, I note that labour unions had almost $7 million invested. Member go on and talk about the big banks being saved when in most instances, when you go through this list, you find it is the ordinary people who are being helped?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to see that information. All we have is a listing by category. We do not have a list of how much individual big banks or big business have deposited in the bank. I do not think he or I were elected to sign a blank cheque. If he were in opposition, he would be getting up and asking the same kinds of questions. Why a blank cheque? speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

October 8, 1985

that it is in power, albeit with another man at the head? All I am asking for is that the Government provide us with a list of those depositors.

Mr. Speaker, I recall that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) urged me very strongly last winter to pay off uninsured depositors in Pioneer Trust. He never once asked for a list of those depositors. Neither did the NDP in the Province of Saskatchewan raise the issue of a list of uninsured depositors when the Government paid those depositors. Oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

These people thought they were insured up to $60,000. It was not one farmer, it was a lot of them.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made quite a thing out of C. D. Howe's remark about a million and I presume he is unfamiliar with what C. D. Howe had to say, which was not that at all. He was being cross-examined by the Hon. Howard Green and what he actually said was:

me?

He was talking about a constant whittling down of trade preferences by the Government. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) just paid tribute to the Conservative attitude over the years and I thought I might repay a small favour.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his contribution. He is a former paperboy in the City of Yorkton and I always listen very closely to his words of wisdom. No doubt that is what C. D. Howe said in the House. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who has been in politics much longer than me, said that C. D. Howe actually said: "What's a million?" in the election campaign of 1957. My comment today was that C. D. Howe was defeated after he said that, and today we have a Government which is saying in effect: "What's a billion?" I think that is wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Opposition is delaying passage of this Bill. That means that the depositors who had confidently invested their money in a Western regional bank will have to wait a long time before being reimbursed.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), who boasted about having our friendship and respect, should know that our respect for him has gone down a lot since he has risen to speak. Mr. Speaker, he says that the big banks, the bigwigs, the very wealthy, will benefit from this legislation. He complains about not having the list of those who will be reimbursed. Yet, the Minister of State for Finance tabled yesterday the list of categories of depositors, and I do not see that many very wealthy people on it. When we look, for instance, at the figures for the municipalities, we see things things like populations of 25,000. I cannot believe that in a village with a population of 25,000, all 25,000 would be very wealthy people.
This small municipality is owed $10 million. An amount of $10 million is a lot for a municipality of 25,000 people.
Another municipality has a population of 50,000. That is even smaller than my city of Gatineau, which is considered an average-size town. This small town is owed $143,000. Then, there is a town with the same population as Gatineau which is owed $4 million.
I can tell the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville that if the town of Gatineau had had the misfortune of investing $4

October, 8 1985
Depositors Compensation
million of the Gatineau taxpayers' money in the Canadian Commercial Bank, there would be a major crisis in the municipality.
In fact, I heard this morning on the radio a financial advisor for the city of Hull who spoke about the investment of this city, which has a population of 55,000 and is therefore a small town, which investment had been recommended by financial experts. The Hull advisor said that the town had been approached by the big chartered bank after people had been encouraged to trust the Canadian Commercial Bank and it was the big bank which told him: Why do you no longer have your deposits with us? Why do you have your deposits with a small regional bank? That is when the City of Hull tried to withdraw part of its investment.
However, there is still at least $5 million in the Canadian Commercial Bank which belong to Hull taxpayers. Yet, I do not believe that these are very wealthy people, Mr. Speaker.
In my opinion, the Hon. Member, whom we used to respect, does not do himself any credit by using such methods and by trying to criticize the Government and to suggest that the decision made last March was ill-advised. He speaks about the list of depositors. He wants the names of those who had deposits with the Canadian Commercial Bank. But would he pass a judgment after receiving such a list? Would he be the one to decide, for instance, that Municipality A and Pension Fund B would be reimbursed, but Labour Union C would not be because it had invested an enormous amount, which means that it is a big union and therefore very wealthy. Does this mean that Union C should not be reimbursed?
How would he choose amongst the mutual funds? Would he choose on the basis of the amount invested? Of the population served? Of the language spoken? Of the size of the area? Of whether the area served is rural or urban? How would he choose?
Mr. Speaker, it is nonsense to ask for a list of depositors before helping all of those who invested in all good faith in the Canadian Commercial Bank.
As recently as yesterday, we saw the lawyers involved with the Estey Commission which is investigating the unfortunate situation of the two banks, and it is very difficult to get access to documents deemed confidential under the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, it is provided for in our conventions that the indentity of depositors and the amounts of their deposits are to be kept confidential. It is a well-known fact that we have a most stable society in which private property and the privacy of citizens are respected. Our banking system, also one of the most stable in the world, requires that sort of confidentiality. When we have expert and legal opinion to the effect that the names of those depositors should not be disclosed, I see no reason why the Opposition could ask us to breach conventions that have been serving us well.
We know full well, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal Party, when they were in power, did breach a number of times and seriously several of those conventions with respect to business matters. This is why confidence of the business community declined to a point where there was tremendous harm done to the economy and an astronomical rise in unemployment. In their Government's energy program the Liberals also failed to show any respect for the business people who are building this country and who were on the point of providing Western Canada with the most remarkable development opportunities.
As far as the New Democratic Party is concerned, they believe that private property is some sort of a sin or crime. Virtue is not being rich, it is being poor. It is indeed because of that lack of respect for business conventions such as for instance the passing of retroactive legislation aimed at people who had invested in confidence in Western Canada's oil development that this country's economy was undermined. So Mr. Speaker, we are once again witnessing an effort, a new attack from the Liberals in the Official Opposition and from the New Democratic Party against conventions that are protecting our economic community and and our quality of life.
With their meddling habits, the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party have developed an attitude that is harmful to the business community and public enterprise. We, who belong to a party that respects private enterprise, private property, and the privacy of citizens, will not accept that, under the guise of feigned outrage, a new attack be launched to once more undermine efforts at protecting private property and the privacy of citizens. This is witchhunting, Mr. Speaker. It is true that those depositors will be getting refunds from the Public Treasury, but they are still entitled to that confidentiality so long as we are not satisfied that there is an essential need to brush it aside. This would then be a most serious precedent, as stated a number of times by witnesses before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. They said that if ever there was a breach of banking confidentiality, then the whole banking system would be endangered. One has but to check the minutes of the Committee to see how concerned they were with the Opposition launching such a witchhunt, using that kind of an excuse.
As far as the Leader of the Official Opposition is concerned, reading from press clippings and Hansard for mid-March, we see that he was absolutely silent on the issue. Maybe he recalled that he represented a Western constituency, or maybe he wanted to act responsibly. It is unfortunate that he has now strayed from that responsible position that honored him last March. We even noted in the speech he made yesterday, that he is trying to backtrack from that first attitude. This in my view is quite typical coming from the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker. He does not seem to be able to stick to his decisions. He suggests they were imposed upon him or,
October 8, 1985

when he finds out that the wind has turned, he makes an about-face.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is almost one p.m., and I would like to continue this afternoon, if you will allow me, rather than being cut right in the middle-
It is time for the Government to accommodate the tourist operators. Bailing out the banks does not build a healthy economy. Supporting a growth industry like tourism does. Listen to what the industry is saying. The tourist operators know what works.

Mr. Speaker, "Tourism Tomorrow" is the title of a conference taking place this week here in Ottawa. Industry and Government have gathered at the Congress Centre to discuss the future of tourism. I too am concerned about what lies ahead for tourism. However, my concerns run through a different vein.
The tourism sector has been hailed as our proudest growth industry. But there will be no tourism industry tomorrow if the Government continues to stymie the efforts of operators across the country. "Change the image of Canada", the Government says. "Give it more sex appeal". This industry needs serious consideration before sex appeal.
How do we convince Canadians to vacation in their own country when the price of gasoline has skyrocketed? By January, 1987, the cost of filling up at the pumps will have jumped 18 cents a gallon. Canadians will stop dead in their tracks when that hits them in the pocket book.
How do we persuade foreigners to explore our vast and diverse regions when the Government is not prepared to launch an effective marketing campaign? It will not spend the dollars to sell our wares in a way that works.
Closer to home, our local operators need assistance to grow and prosper. They are small business people. Provide them with what it takes to ensure that tourists return to our rugged regions year after year.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) is treating the Province of Nova Scotia in particular as a poor orphan.
Unbelievably, without any replacement or alternatives, she announced the end of the Petroleum Incentives Program, or PIP grants, which had sparked offshore drilling for gas and oil. Either in business terms or public policy terms, it is totally unacceptable to pull the plug without an alternative plan.
Uncertainty will kill hopes for prosperity from offshore gas development. Companies must plan, even if the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources does not. Drilling projects are ending, leases are expiring and, give it another month or so, companies will leave and not come back.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised "jobs, jobs, jobs" and economic development for Atlantic Canada. However, the September report of Informetrica predicts a loss of jobs and no production from the Venture development. That would be a tragedy.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker. No PIP, no alternatives, no hurry, and no concern. Why has the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who was such a Santa Claus with the Western Accord, become such a Scrooge to Nova Scotia? Surely Nova Scotia deserves more than this foggy silence from the Minister.

subtopic: ISRAEL-CONDEMNATION OF AIR RAID ON TUNIS AND OF PALESTINIAN TERRORISTS
ISRAEL-CONDEMNATION OF AIR RAID ON TUNIS AND OF PALESTINIAN TERRORISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bombing and devastation of Tunis last week by the State of Israel was in direct violation of the Geneva and Hague conventions as well as of the United Nations Charter to which both Israel and Canada are signatories.
The terrorist activities by a dissident group of Palestinians in piracy on the high seas, as well as the murder of innocent Israelis in Egypt, can no doubt be tied into the bombing.
The attack on Tunisia resulted in the death of women and children, not by a phantom terrorist group, claimed by no one,

October 8, 1985
but by the most sophisticated armed force in the world-the State of Israel.
Canada, as a respected and peaceful nation and as a friend of Tunisia, Egypt, and Israel, should not hestitate to indicate our disgust with the unlawful incursion on the sovereignty of Tunisia, the murder of innocent civilians in Egypt, and the terrorist piracy by a fanatical few Palestinians.
I urge the Government to move as soon as possible to raise a motion of censure and condemnation in the United Nations of the State of Israel as being in willful and direct violation of the ninth and tenth Conventions of the Hague and Geneva and United Nations Charter, in concert with a motion of condemnation of the terrorist activities of Palestinians against innocent people of any nationality.

subtopic: HUNTING AND TRAPPING-SUSPENSION OF GREENPEACE ANTI-FUR CAMPAIGN
HUNTING AND TRAPPING-SUSPENSION OF GREENPEACE ANTI-FUR CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the decision by Greenpeace to suspend their European anti-fur campaign and trust that this signifies a new appreciation of the importance of hunting and trapping to Canada's aboriginal peoples. We are proud of the success which Indigenous Survival International has achieved, particularly through the efforts of its co-chairman, Mr. Georges Erasmus.
Canada's native peoples have enjoyed a harmonious relationship with nature for thousands of years. Indigenous Survival International promotes an awareness that cultural survival for native peoples depends upon their right to hunt, trap and fish. Our Government believes in the sustainable use of the world's renewable resources and encourages the efforts of Indigenous Survival International to promote the wise conservation of these resources.
While this recent success by ISI is encouraging, it is only a beginning. Much work remains to be done before other groups realize that their anti-fur crusades threaten to destroy native peoples and their cultures.
I am confident that the Government of Canada will continue to support the right of native peoples to pursue their traditional ways of life.

Mr. Speaker, I have with me thousands of petitions signed by mothers protesting the Government's decision to cut S55 million from income support programs for families with children, and more specifically, to de-index family allowances.

subtopic: PREPAYMENT OF TAX BY SENIOR CITIZENS HOLDING CANADA SAVINGS BONDS
PREPAYMENT OF TAX BY SENIOR CITIZENS HOLDING CANADA SAVINGS BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to inform Hon. Members of the House of a situation which was brought to my attention by several senior citizens in my riding of Brandon-Souris. As we are aware, many senior citizens invest a large portion of their savings in Canada Savings Bonds. However, as income tax is not deducted from interest payments, or from most other sources of income for seniors, that income tax frequently must be prepaid on a quarterly basis, even though interest from those bonds is not received until November.
Unfortunately, it is often quite difficult for many senior citizens to do their own calculations on the amount of interest they will receive and on the amount their payments must be. Furthermore, they fail to understand why they must make income tax payments on money which is yet to be received.
Perhaps, to alleviate some of these problems, income tax could be automatically deducted from interest payments on bonds as it is from RRSP pay-outs, or perhaps bond holders might be able to have their interest paid on a quarterly basis as well. Certainly in an age of electronic banking this could be an option. Failing these reforms, the least that could be done to ease the situation would be to ask the Government to issue a statement, or a bill, to senior citizens reminding them of when to pay and calculating that payment for them.
Senior citizens in Canada are not opposed to paying their fair share of income tax, but they do not feel that that tax should be paid until the income is actually received.

Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members of Parliament are no doubt aware of the terrible drought which affected southern Saskatchewan or the southern Prairies last summer. Now we have the double disaster of a drought on one hand and rain and snow on the other hand, so that the grain in the fields is lying under snow and cannot be harvested.
Last summer, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) asked the Hon. Mr. Speaker, in concluding this morning, I said it was unfortunate that the Leader of the Opposition had relinquished the responsible ways he had shown so well last March when he supported the rescue plan.
I read in an article in the Edmonton Journal that what the Leader of the Opposition, claimed, was unfounded and I quote:

October 8, 1985

"It's unlikely that the Canadian Commercial Bank pumped $300 million into its U.S. subsidiary, as charged by Liberal Leader John Turner, a California banking regulator said Wednesday. "To my knowledge, there was no such infusion of funds", said David Scott, California deputy superintendent of banks "Remember that Westlands only has $386 million of assets in total"."

Mr. Speaker, this reminds me of a statement made by the Leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister, when he said that the Progressive Conservative Party was going to fire 600,000 public servants as soon as we were elected, although everybody knew perfectly well we only had 258,000 public servants in Canada. So there was some amateur exaggeration involved, and unfortunately, the Leader of the Opposition is now resuming this practice.
Journalists, whom the Leader of the Opposition quotes with such authority and relish, also had a few things to say, namely that the Government had no choice but to lend a helping hand to this regional bank so as to safeguard its deposits and also avoid hurting the economy of Western Canada which was slow to recoup and was in fact lagging behind the rest of the country's economic recovery. 1 would like to quote here from a column by John Ferguson of Southam News, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on March 26, 1985, the day after the rescue plan for the Canadian Commercial Bank was announced. He said, and I quote:
"The continuing problems faced by the Canadian Commercial Bank underline the fact that the economic recovery is still very uneven, with the West lagging well behind the rest of the country. A major part of the Commercial Bank's problems are the result of the large number of poor loans it has in western Canada, much of the money loaned to the oil and gas industry or for home mortgages during the boom years".

He went on to say:

"Money that would have been paid to the debenture holders out of future bank profits now will increase the Commercial Bank cash flow making it more likely the banks and the governments will get paid back".

Mr. Speaker, people really thought the rescue plan would succeed. This journalist also had the following to say, and I quote:

"Allowing the ten-year-old bank to go under would have negative impact on financial markets, possibly even with some effect on the value of the dollar. Finally, if the Commercial Bank had gone under, there would have been losses to several pension fund investors. Quebec's Caisse de Depot, which
invests money for the Quebec Pension plan, held 10 per cent ownership according to a 1983 prospectus filed by the bank. The Canadian National Rail pension fund, the Air Canada pension trust, the Alberta Government Telephone pension fund, and the Alberta Teachers' retirement fund also would have lost out if the bank had been allowed to go under".
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that a decision had been made, and even our journalist who does not have a reputation for being particularly soft on this Government admitted that the decision was a sound one. However, Mr. Speaker, a few weeks later, at a meeting of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, some doubts were raised about this measure which had been taken to help the regional bank, and they were raised by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), which led the chairman of the board of directors of the Canadian Commercial Bank, Mr. Paul Paine, to complain in June that the proceedings of the committee on which this particular Member was sitting had undermined the public's confidence in the Bank during the rescue period. I would like to quote from an article in the Calgary Herald of June 14, by David Triguero, where he says, and 1 quote:

"Paine emphasized that CCB management practice had been approved and supported by William Kennett, Federal Inspector General of Banks, and Gerald Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada, who may be described as 'all people of high degree of independent credibility and people who understand banking'. Its critics, on the other hand, 'are not terribly familiar with banking and could not be expected to learn much in the few short sessions that the committee heard evidence' ".

However, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Trinity had already raised doubts about the rescue operations. Lack of responsibility, Mr. Speaker? It is not surprising that the rescue plan did not succeed.
Another subject is that of deregulation of the banking system.

A very good part of this debate, Mr. Speaker, should focus on Liberal inaction on regulatory reform for the last 16 years. Even John Evans, former Liberal Chairman of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, admitted last week on the CBC that the previous Government was well aware of the problems vis-a-vis financial institution regulations, and yet did not act. Our Government, Mr. Speaker, on the contrary, is committed to regulatory reform and has indicated so in the Throne Speech, the economic statement, the Wyman Report, and a discussion paper on financial institutions. Earlier, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) asked why we did not do anything immediately. The reason for that is that we were busy mopping up the mess that the Liberals left us; a mess of unemployment, high interest rates, and a large deficit.
October 8, 1985



Mr. Speaker, eleven institutions were operating in Canada when the Bank Act was revised in 1980. After that, the number jumped to 70, which means that 59 new institutions began to operate after the revision of the Bank Act, yet no effort was made by the previous administration to change the regulations.
So Mr. Kennett had to make do with what was there when the Canadian Commercial Bank problem arose.
Why did the Liberals fail to make the necessary changes? Perhaps they were too busy trying to thwart the western petroleum industry which was about to show that it no longer needed to depend on the central Government.
For instance we know that Mr. Lalonde's philosophy was that the central Government had to be very strong, intervene in everything, and tell the regions how and when to develop.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, instead of backing the winners they were bleeding the winners. That is why we found ourselves in a situation where a bank that was doing very well in the boom years suddenly found itself in difficulty. Today we are faced with the results of the bad administration which we suffered for almost 20 years, and we want to help its victims. However, we are told by the same Liberal Party and by the same NDP, which supported the energy program and several other policies that were so detrimental to the West, that they cannot have their money, that they are big, rich and powerful, even though they are small municipalities, small credit unions, and small insurance companies. Somebody somewhere has a life insurance policy on a loved one and would probably depend on the insurance money to raise a family if a tragedy happened. However, the money is tied up in the Canadian Commercial Bank and we are not allowed to give them relief because they are considered to be very rich people.

Again, Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said earlier. 1 think that the request for a list of depositors is nonsense. 1 think it is immoral to want to intervene in the private life of Canadians. And I think it is about time this Bill be adopted by the House. We have wasted enough time and must get back to work immediately, as we began to do, on a review of the banking regulations and give the Inspector of Banks the tools he needs to ensure that our banking system remains sound.
