speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) is going to stay near her seat, because we have a few things to say to each other. In any case, 1 would like to read to her the last paragraph, since I only have a minute, of the editorial that appeared in the Edmonton Journal on October 2, 1985, which reads as follows:

"Principles lost in bank fiasco". It states, "By trying to blame the Liberals for the collapse of the Canadian Commercial
October 8, 1985

Bank and Northland Bank, the Government shows it is bankrupt of any sense of responsibility for its actions".

Mr. Speaker, in taking this opportunity to speak to Bill C-79 and especially to the amendment. I would simply like to clarify the issue and start by saying that the amendment before the House is what is referred to as a reasoned amendment and objects to the principle contained in Bill C-79. The House will recall the amendment was moved by the Leader of my party, Mr. Turner, and seconded by myself, and it reads as follows: "this House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public monies to unspecified persons or corporations, thereby substantially denigrating Parliamentary accountability for expenditure of public funds."
Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing we do in this House, it is that we are accountable to our constituents and to Canadians in general, and in this respect, I think it is very important that the federal Government, with the spending powers it has, should be able at all times to justify its expenditures and do so publicly.
The purpose of Bill C-79 being considered today is to authorize the expenditure of $875 million to compensate uninsured depositors who had invested money with the Canadian Commercial Bank, the Northland Bank and the CCB Mortgages Investment Corporation, and all this without revealing the names of the people who stand to benefit from this legislation. The legislation is of course meant to compensate over and above the usual $60,000 paid to any Canadian depositor in a bank that is a member of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. In other words, Canadians are insured for up to $60,000 by public funds, an insurance fund to which we contribute a percentage of our deposits.
Mr. Speaker, all the editorials I have in front of me obviously repeat the same thing. I am going to read one that appeared in the Toronto Star on October 7, which reads as follows:
"How on earth can the Progressive Conservative Government continue to argue that Canadians should not be told the names of depositors in two failed western banks who are being bailed out with public money? A Government Bill asks Parliament to approve an $875 million public expenditure to finance the bail-out but it ignores the taxpayers' right to know where their money will go".

Mr. Speaker, that is what the argument is essentially about. Why not release the list of uninsured depositors covered by this legislation?

Are they trying to pass the buck? Is the Government saying what it said in March of this year when it requested money from taxpayers to save the Canadian Commercial Bank which indeed failed? At that time we had to trust the Government
Depositors Compensation
and have confidence in it. Should its continued stonewalling on the issue to date require from us an act of faith or an act of good will? Should we tell the Government to go ahead and spend close to $1 billion without telling us where the money is going? On the basis of its lack of disclosure, we ask the Government today to come clean and tell us who is covered or who will benefit. Confidence in the Government is not enhanced by stonewalling on its part.

Mr. Speaker, last March, the Government told the House: "Quick, something must be done, it is very urgent and our banking system is in peril. One of our banks is in trouble. Now be nice and adopt the Bill, without too much debate, please, and you are going to be asked to give us your support, because trust us, this measure is going to help make viable one of our banking institutions, the Canadian Commercial Bank."
Mr. Speaker, we all know this was false, that the Government had failed to do its homework, that it misled the Canadian people, that it spoke without sufficient knowledge of the facts, without having the requisite studies on the table, studies that should have been done. It misled us, and the result is that $255 million were spent in March 1985, and that today, they are asking us for another $875 million-

In Bill C-79, the Government is asking for $875 million, as 1 said. In my riding of Ottawa-Vanier, $875 million is a lot of money. I have been asked by constituents to whom these moneys are going. Will it go to the poor, the unemployed, elderly people, widows or women living below the poverty line? The answer is no. Will the money be used for economically deprived children in our schools to better feed and clothe them? Again the answer is no. This huge sum of money, this king's ransom, will be used to bail out uninsured depositors of two chartered banks which the Government allowed to die. More important, this Bill will bail out not only two banks but two Ministers, two incompetent Ministers-the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). That is what the Bill does. It bails them out. It gives them an out on the backs of taxpayers.
I remind the House and the people who are listening today that both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance assured the House on numerous occasions in debate, in Committee of the Whole and repeatedly in Question Period, that both banks would be or could be kept in business.
I return to the magnitude of the sum involved. I have done some calculations. Since it is not going to the poor or to the elderly, since it is not going to clothe and feed children, I asked myself with what people would identify when considering $875 million. It could mean 28 million family allowance cheques of $31.27. It could mean 3.1 million Old Age Security cheques of $282.94 per month. It could mean 2.6 million Guaranteed Income Security payments or 1.5 million spousal allowance payments. The $875 million is not going to the poor or to the elderly. It is going to bail out people who, by the admission of many specialists, benefited from an investment which was

October 8, 1985

superior to the going market rate. They took that money, and I hope they took the risk; they should bear the brunt. One cannot argue, as the Government is doing, that this is a precedent. If it happens in a year or so from now, the Government will say that it could not be anticipated and hide behind ignorance of the facts.
I should like to refer to the City of Ottawa and to put the $875 million into perspective once again. The City of Ottawa raises approximately $300 million per year in taxes. In fact, the exact figures for 1985 are as follows: municipal taxes, $66,527,600; regional taxes, $81,834,600; school taxes, separate and public combined, $143,052,000, for a grand total of $291,414,200. The total tax collected by the City of Vanier in the year 1985 was $11,268,000. If we combine the taxes for the City of Ottawa and for the City of Vanier, $875 million would mean no taxes for a period of three years. At the going rate of interest of 8 or 9 per cent today, it is a phenomenal amount of money.

speechtext:
I will deal with the shareholders, but right now I am trying to explain-and the Hon. Member would not understand that-what $875 million means in my riding. I will talk about the shareholders, because it is an interesting point. On the question of depositors and shareholders I wrote to the Minister in April-and I do not know if the Hon. Member did that-because I was concerned. We had participated in a very serious debate here, so I wrote to the Minister on April 22 asking her specifically what were the commitments of the Canadian Commercial Bank with regard to the proportion of the bank's business in Canadian and United States loans. I also asked the Minister about ownership, for a list of shareholders showing the number of shares held, and so on.
On May 21, 1985 the Minister answered and supplied me with a profile of deposits showing at least $635 million of deposits. I also saw in the answer she gave me a profile of the loan portfolios and something which I thought rather interesting, the major common shareholders and major preferred shareholders. Up until now we have failed to talk much about shareholders and I would like to address that point since I was invited to do so by the Hon. Member.
The common shareholders were pension trust funds, and I can name them all: Air Canada pension trust fund; Alberta Government telephone employees trust fund; the Teacher's Retirement Fund of Alberta; la Caisse de depot du Placement du Quebec; the CNR pension trust fund; the CBC-I even find in there the City of Ottawa superannuation fund, 106,086
common shares-down the drain-they have lost it, pretty well. What were those shares worth in March as compared to today? There is a whole list of shareholders which I would be glad to submit to anyone who is interested. I only have 20 minutes so I do not want to read this into the record. I have already made this public so people can have access to this document if they so desire. The reason I am talking about the magnitude of $875 million is, as stated in the reasoned amendment before us, that we on this side object to paying out $875 million to unknown depositors. We object to being asked again by this Government to perform blindly an act of faith.
I asked myself when I first saw this, why would the Government have what we would call-
[ Translation]
-a special bill. Why did the Government introduce such a bill in the House when we are all aware that the Winding-up Act could perfectly apply to the failure of a bank. I believe it is Section 87 of the Winding-up Act which provides that when a creditor wants to submit a claim, he or she must do so openly and publicly. Section 97(7) of the Bankruptcy Act, which does not apply to banks, but does apply in all other cases, provides for something similar. Whoever wants to be reimbursed must publicly submit a claim to a receiver, providing him with his or her name, the amount claimed and all the necessary evidence in support of the claim.
1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, why do we have before us a bill which exceptionally changes the rules of the game. For instance, Clause 3 states that the Minister of Finance may, on application in the prescribed form and manner, make payment to the depositor of an amount equal to so much of the deposit-
Mr. Speaker, the Government had to find a way out, because the Winding-up Act, which applies to Banks, and the Bankruptcy Act, which does not, would both have compelled it to provide the names of all the creditors who have so far submitted claims to the curator or the receiver. Mr. Speaker, that is the purpose of our amendment to the legislation we are dealing with today. We want to know who the depositors are, as it is our duty to do so, that we may say to our constituents: The depositors are simply Mr. or Mrs. so and so, this and that corporation, this or that financial institution, this or that foreign bank, for they have submitted claims to the curator or the receiver.

When speaking to the main motion, I will want to review the history and the reasons why we voted for this promise of a bail-out in March and why today we are so mad-that is the word-at a Government that did not play ball as seriously as it should have. We were asked to restore confidence by performing an act of faith in the Government's proposal. I have a chronology of events here. The Government had not even asked the external auditors what was going on in the CCB. It had not even bothered to ask experts in the banking field, although the banks offered voluntarily to do it. The banks said.
October 8, 1985

"We will examine the portfolio of loans and we will tell you". This was in March, before this fiasco occurred, and the Government said no.
By refusing to do the elementary and serious investigation that it should have done it put Canadians as a whole, taxpayers specifically, and Members of Parliament in a situation where we have a Bill before us that proposes to bailout two banks, Canadian Commercial and Northland.
Northland is an entity by itself that was brought in, dragged in, pushed in, or packaged by this Government. We all remember the famous interview that Mr. Neapole gave on TV when he said that this Government wanted to destroy him. Here is a president of a bank accusing this Government, several weeks before, saying that the Government is out to get him. I would like to speak on that on the main motion, but I think I made my point on the $875 million and why this reasoned amendment has to be approved by this House. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

I would like to ask him a question. How would he make the difference, simply looking at a list of depositors, in order to decide who is going to be compensated and who is not to be, with compensation based on the financial status of the person or the institution that made the deposit with the Commercial Bank of Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I am looking, for instance, at a list that was supplied by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDou-gall), where, if banks, whether Schedule A or B banks or Trust Companies are eliminated, there are at least $123 million of investments that would be lost if the Bill were not to pass.
And by coincidence, he mentioned that the City of Vanier, I believe, had some $11 million in tax revenues. Looking at the first two classes of municipalities, those with populations of

25,000 and 50,000, and I think this is about the size of the municipality he is representing, that totals $11 million.
In other words, we would ask a municipality like Vanier to relinquinsh some $11 million, unless we make a choice from that list. How would he go about making that choice?
Moreover, looking at individuals, at the $60,000-$99,999 deposit levels, I am saying that individuals who invested that kind of money may be pensioners who sold their family house and invested the money in that bank, in order to have subsist-ance income, to enjoy a secure retirement in later years. At that point, are we to decide that those are rich people and that we will not compensate them, simply because the figure here exceeds $60,000? Tell me, Mr. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), how would you make the difference? Whom would you compensate, and whom would you not compensate?

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Vanier (Mr. Gauthier).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two points were raised by the Hon. Member for Gatineau. First, whether banks are inspected and how that is done.
I can say that regarding the inspection of the Canadian Commercial Bank, and this is the opinion of the Committee of the House that examined the bankruptcy question, and I refer to what was reported in the proceedings of the Committee, namely that the history of the CCB has been marked by a series of imprudent loans, dubious accounting policies, inadequate disclosure of information and deficient supervision. That says it all.
Even if inspection was carried out, if accounting policies are dubious, loans imprudent and disclosure is inadequate, it seems to me that says it all. It was the bank's own poor administrative practice which caused it to collapse.
As for the second question raised by the Hon. Member, I think she made an important point. Of course municipalities are anxious to recover their deposits. I would be the first to agree. I would say to the Hon. Member: Let these municipalities say so publicly. Thus far, and the Hon. Member knows as well as I do, Kanata has said: We have $9 million in the Canadian Commercial Bank. Everybody knows that today. This is one of the municipalities with a population of between 50,000 and 100,000, perhaps a bit more, but in any case, it has $9 million on deposit with the Canadian Commercial Bank.
It is also a fact, and it was said publicly, that St. Catharines in Ontario was in the same position. Toronto as well. Hull had a few million dollars. Some municipalities, and I know munic-

October 8, 1985
Depositors Compensation
ipal affairs as well as I do education, had made a habit of investing in debentures and other investments with these banks because their rates were a quarter or half a point higher.
I do not know whether the Hon. Member for Gatineau saw the interview with the Mayor of Kanata on the weekend. She told the public clearly what her position was, which one had some trouble accepting as a valid reason. She said: "Our administrators have a mandate to invest the municipality's revenues at the best going rate, for as long as we do not need those monies". I would say to the Hon. Member for Gatineau, that if interest rates had gone down and if the investment in question had been discussed by the Mayor at that time, perhaps her administrators would have been more prudent. Now the Mayor has publicly admitted that Kanata has changed its investment methods as a result of this unfortunate experience, and that it will no longer be left up to the discretion of the select few to decide what should be done with public monies.
I think there is a lesson here for municipalities to be more careful and to be a little less, I do not want to say demanding but they will have to be a little more reasonable. And they should not invest in high risk situations. Of course the rate is higher. The profits are higher. But if the risk is greater, it means you might lose your shirt. I am not saying that the municipalities of Kanata and St. Catharines and Toronto, which are public bodies, should lose their deposits. I am just saying that all these municipalities should have the good grace to tell us publicly tomorrow morning who they are. And why not do so on a voluntary basis? I urge all depositors to do so, to make this information public before the House, by sending a letter to the Clerk of the House saying: I am a depositor, I have x dollars on deposit. What is wrong with that, what is wrong with saying these things in public, with saying: 1 want to be helped with public funds, and 1 am in a position, and am agreeable to, releasing that information?
I think that is the solution. I say to the Hon. Member for Gatineau that neither of us can vote blindfold, our ears muffled and our mouths shut. There is a fishy smell, but the fact remains that Members of this House will have to remember that when they spend money, they are to be accountable to their constituents. That is the answer to the question.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I think I answered that question in my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I said we had been misled, that perhaps we had been dragged into the operation without realizing its full impact. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret, but questions and comments are over. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

Mr. Speaker, we are now being asked to call upon the people of Canada to put $875 million into the winding up of the affairs of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. We ought to remember that this is not the first such request made of this House. We ought to remember that in March, Parliament agreed, over the objections of members of the New Democratic Party, to put $225 million into the failing bank. We were told by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that if that $225 million was made available, the Canadian Commercial Bank would become a viable operation.
These two banks are the first in recent history to find themselves in this kind of trouble. However, in recent years, financial institutions and trust companies have got into trouble. Indeed, from 1980 on, 17 trust companies went bankrupt. We learned today that another trust company in Alberta is no longer financially viable.
This morning when I asked the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) a question about the responsibility of the former Liberal Government which did not set up a system to protect the people against failures of trust companies, he said that all or most of these failed trust companies were operating under provincial charters and therefore the then Liberal federal Government was not responsible. However, we have a federal corporation called the Canada Deposit Corporation which was set up to guarantee people who have deposits in trust companies and banks that they will not lose their money if they have less than $60,000 on deposit. This is a Crown corporation which has already had to pay out well over $1 billion. Since the Crown corporation, in the process of dealing with trust companies which became insolvent, now owns $1.5
October 8, 1985

billion worth of property, surely the former Government ought to have begun to ask what was wrong with our financial institutions. We cannot blame this Conservative Government for the failure of the former Government to bring in legislation to set up a system which would regulate and protect the people who deposit money in financial institutions.
However, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance told the people of Canada in March that if $225 million was provided to help the Canadian Commercial Bank it would become a viable operation. We have to ask ourselves on what basis they said that. Don McGillivray, who writes a regular column in the Southam papers, in an article which appeared in The Citizen of Ottawa in September asked: "Who pays for the crash of the Canadian Commercial Bank?" He said that it would be the ordinary Canadians. About the present situation and the amount of money required, he said, "it need not have been so large if the bank regulators had been watching more closely and the Government had not tried to pump life into a bank which was clinically dead in March". Don McGillivray is correct. In fact, in March, that bank was dead. It could not be revived.
How did the Government conclude in March that it should try to keep that bank going? The Government depended upon the Inspector General of Banks and the Governor of the Bank of Canada. If the Government did not know in March that the advice it was receiving was bad, then it certainly should have known in May and June. In May and June the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs heard representations regarding the CCB from bank officials, the Inspector General of Banks, auditors of the banks and the Governor of the Bank of Canada. The evidence in that regard was damning. It was clear that the advice given to the Government belief was all wrong. It was clear that the Canadian Commercial Bank could not survive. I say that if the Government did not know in March it was receiving bad advice from the Inspector General of Banks, then it should have known in May and June. It should certainly know now when it is asking the people of Canada to put up substantially more than $1 billion to take care of the mistakes made by those officials and by the Government.
I would like to deal for a moment with the Inspector General of Banks. Several years before the news in 1985 about the CCB's difficulties, he was told by the Superintendent of Insurance that Leonard Rosenberg, who was so instrumental in creating one of the largest disasters in the field of trust companies which this country has ever seen, was involved in wheeling and dealing with the then President of the Canadian Commercial Bank, Mr. Eaton. This was several years before it became apparent that the bank was in grave trouble and that it was involved in very questionable financial dealings. Indeed, at one point, Mr. Rosenberg, or Mr. Rosenberg and his family, controlled probably more than twice as many of the shares of the bank as are permitted to be held under the provisions of the Bank Act. Surely, the Inspector General of Banks should have been aware of what was happening. Surely he should
Depositors Compensation
have taken notice. Surely he should have been monitoring the operations of the Canadian Commercial Bank on a careful and day-to-day basis. He did not do that. When he appeared before the Finance committee he said that when he looked at the operations of the bank in trying to find out about the poor loans, loans which were probably never to be repaid, he depended almost exclusively on the information which he received from the officers of the bank and bank employees.
There was another occasion when the Inspector General of Banks should have been put on notice. I would like to quote one short paragraph from page 6 of the June report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which reads:
On October 12, 1983, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) issued a "Cease and Desist Order" against the Westlands Bank. The FDIC cited numerous reasons for the order, including hazardous lending, lax collection practices, large volume of poor quality loans, inadequate liquidity, inadequate equity capital and reserves, inadequate loan loss provision, large overhead expenses and poor management.
The Westlands Bank was 100 per cent owned by the Canadian Commercial Bank. It started with a minority share of that bank. However, when it was told by the American regulatory authorities that the Westlands bank was in some difficulty and that the authorities were not satisfied with the way the bank was operating, the Canadian Commercial Bank moved to take 100 per cent control of the bank. Surely, in 1983, when the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation of the United States issued that cease and desist order, the Inspector General of Banks should have been on notice that he had to keep a very careful eye on the Canadian Commercial Bank. He seemed not to pay any attention to that. He did virtually nothing until he was told in 1985 that the bank needed a major infusion of financial help or it would be forced to close down.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada intervened in the CCB situation. In 1983 he did something which was unprecedented. He called The Globe and Mail and said that, in his view, the Canadian Commercial Bank was a viable operation. Indeed, while the Finance committee was holding its hearings in May and June, and after the committee had heard from the officials of the bank, the Inspector General and the auditors about all the things which had gone wrong with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the dishonest way in which it had acted on some occasions, the Governor of the Bank of Canada told the committee that he still had confidence that the then officers of the bank could mount a viable operation.
I ask Hon. Members to compare those statements of the Governor of the Bank of Canada with a speech he made just a few days ago on September 25 in Toronto when he said:
The Bank of Canada ... is not involved in monitoring the Financial soundness of individual banks and supervising their behaviour. Parliament has not given us that responsibility or the powers that would enable us to fulfil that function. The Bank of Canada has no bank auditors, no bank examiners, no power to require details of individual loans, deposits or any other kind of private transaction.
If the Bank of Canada does not have the type of power about which the Governor of the bank spoke a few days ago, whey then did he intervene in 1983 and again in the spring of

October 8, 1985
Depositors Compensation
this year to tell the people of Canada that he considered the bank to be a viable operation?
We have heard a great deal from Hon. Members on the Government side about the difficulties the credit unions, municipalities and pension funds would be in if this money were not approved. We are told how much money they will lose if they, as uninsured depositors, do not get their money. However, I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that a large part of the reason those organizations left their money on deposit in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank was that they were assured by the Inspector General of Banks, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance that these were viable operations. When these organizations receive that kind of advice from senior Ministers and from senior public servants, who can blame them for leaving their money in those banks? In the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs back in May and June we heard from the auditors of the bank. The Bank Act requires banks to have two set of external auditors. The Canadian Commercial Bank had two of the most prestigious auditing firms in this country and, indeed, if I am not mistaken, they are international auditors with offices in many countries. The amazing thing and, to me, the most disturbing of what we have heard is that the auditors had one set of opinions about the Canadian Commercial Bank which they gave to the directors of the bank, and another set of opinions which they gave to the bank and which the bank use publicly in its annual report. What was said by the committee about the audit report to the officers and directors of the bank appears on page 17 of the report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs: The Committee asks, and I quote:
Did the annual report of CCB for 1984 represent a fair and accurate view of the Bank's financial position at the time?
The report continues, and I quote:
-the total size of the Bank's marginal loans revealed through the support agreement constitute sufficient evidence for the Committee to question the auditors' decision to issue an unqualified opinion.
That was done. The report continues:
However, the auditors also knew that the financial statements approved by them would be used not only by CCB's existing shareholders, but also potential shareholders, creditors and potential creditors.
I do not have the time to quote the auditor's report to the bank directors, but many of the business practices of the bank were questioned. There were a great number of questions in committee about the fact that the bank was given an opinion by the auditors that it was a viable operation which the bank could use in its annual report.
We have to ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, what about the directors of the bank? There were some very prestigious leaders of the business community who were directors of the bank, for instance, the former Premier of Manitoba, Mr. Sterling Lyon. What were the directors doing except taking the fees which were paid to them? Did they not have a responsibility to the depositors, to the shareholders and to the
public to see that the bank was operating in a sensible and prudent way? Obviously not, Mr. Speaker, because except for a few who resigned very quietly because they were dissatisfied with the way the bank was operating, the directors simply took their money and kept quiet.
What about the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, Mr. Speaker? As I have indicated, over a period of a few years it was made responsible to pay out $1.5 billion because of the losses of the trust companies. Surely, it has a responsibility in this case. I say that the Government acted without sufficient knowledge. It ignored the offer of the chartered banks to send in their experienced personnel who could and would have looked at the real situation of the Canadian Commercial Bank and told the Government what was needed. The Government acted with haste, and without care and in an irresponsible way and we certainly are not going to support this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), has reiterated for the past few minutes the inadequacies of the present banking system. I want to assure him that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) totally agrees with him. When our Party came into Government 13 months ago, we inherited a system which was totally inadequate. The Minister of State for Finance has put her mind to reviewing the whole mandate of the Inspector General and seeing that the system is reviewed.
I also want to suggest to my hon. friend that regional banks are extremely important to western Canada. They tend to facilitate small and medium sized businesses. Between 80 per cent and 85 per cent of jobs are created through small business and our Government is out to support jobs. Our main platform is to increase the economy and to put people back to work. The Hon. Member has to realize that regional banks are extremely important and this Government realizes that western Canada did, perhaps, suffer a great downturn when the National Energy Program was brought in by the Liberal Government in 1980. The small banks have suffered due to the National Energy Program but the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has incorporated the Western Accord as of last March and things are on an upturn out West. However, if we had not undergone the severe limitation of the PGRT which caused so many of our rigs to leave western Canada: Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, perhaps these banks would never have gotten into that position.
I would like to ask my hon. friend a question with respect to releasing the names of the uninsured depositors. Would he be in favour of having his personal financial status made public to Canadian citizens? Also, would he like his income tax return made public?

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions but I will do my best to deal with them. Firt, as a resident of a western city, Winnipeg, I am all in favour of regional financial institutions. However, I only favour them if they are operated efficiently, honestly and with sound business principles. I am opposed to any financial institution which is run as sloppily, as
October 8, 1985

carelessly and as dishonestly as the Canadian Commercial Bank.
The Hon. Member says that the Minister recognizes the need for a better system of regulation. I say to the Hon. Member that the Minister may say that, but the Minister is proposing a big expansion of financial institutions to let the trust companies and the insurance companies get into the banking business. The Hon. Member should note the comments made by the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) a few moments ago who pointed out that the State of New York has 300 people working in the Government department which monitors the operations of its financial institutions. 1 will wait with a great deal of interest but not much hope to see whether this Government, which is so determined to downsize virtually every one of its Departments, will be prepared to hire the people required to monitor our financial institutions. It was one thing to have a small monitoring agency when we had only the big five Banks. They are so powerful that even if they make some bad loans they can carry the loss. It is another thing entirely if we are going to have the kind of competition and the large number of institutions which the Hon. Member referred to. The Hon. Member also said that the Canadian Commercial Bank got into trouble because of the National Energy Program. If she reads the evidence she will know that the bank got into trouble not because of the NEP, but because of some very bad investments, including the Westlands Bank.
Today's newspapers talk about the virtual stoppage of exploration for oil and gas off the Atlantic coast. If that continues, I wonder what the spokespersons for this Government will say. They will not be able to blame that situation on the former Liberal Government because it is their Government and their policies which are in place at a time when the oil and gas exploration off the Atlantic coast is being virtually stopped.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to clarify a couple of points with the Hon. Member. He seems to be mixing the Nova Scotia agreement with the Western Accord. They are two separate entities. One covers exploration and development on Canada Lands and the other concerns provincial lands and the two must not be mixed together. As well, he said he did not hold out much hope for a review of the banking system by the Minister. I want him to know that he should have a lot of hope because the Minister realizes that the Inspector General does not have the authority to go in and review and supervise all operations of banks which appear or might appear to be in some difficulty. He will see some changes in the Bank Act and increased activity in the area of inspection in the banking system so we can move forward and not have any further developments along these lines.

speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 46 it is my duty to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canada Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate. I read very carefully the speech made by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) in the House yesterday, and I did not find much of any substance.
Mr. Speaker, I did find what we call in English, and sometimes in French as well, a canard, in fact four canards. And I am not referring to the French word for a particular fowl, but to the word "canard" according to my English dictionary, where a "canard" ...

I would like to refer to The Oxford Dictionary because it is used frequently in English in this context. It says that a canard is an absurd, extravagant rumour or report or hoax. Of course-

-in French the same meaning can be applied to this word, but it is also a commonly known bird-

October 8, 1985
Depositors Compensation

Well, a duck will fly but I can say that the arguments put forward by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall) in support of Bill C-79 will not fly. None of these canards will fly and it is for that reason that I rise to support the amendment to the Bill proposed yesterday by my Leader.
I am a little tired, and I expect you are as well, Mr. Speaker, of hearing speaker after speaker on the Tory benches rise to blame the problems of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank on the previous Government and the National Energy Program. There is truly a canard which will not fly. Canadians are too smart to swallow that kind of nonsense at this stage and I really cannot believe that deep in their heart of hearts, and I include my friend from Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow), Members opposite really think that this situation has been well managed by this Government. Nor do I think that the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, who is in this House today, thinks that this situation has been well managed by the Government. 1 know, Party discipline being what it is, that they will be reluctant to speak out for fear of receiving a call from the Prime Minister's Office. However, no one can accept the rationale put forward by my friend, the Minister of State for Finance. What did she tell us yesterday? She said, and I refer to page 7371 of Hansard-.
We are compensating these depositors because the situation facing these two banks reflects unique and particular circumstances.
Well, true, bad management existed but is that unique? It is not unique in the case of any financial institution which fails. Bad loans, are they unique? The only unique thing in this whole affair was the way in which the Government mismanaged the situation and made misrepresentations to the Canadian public and this House as to the viability of the banks. I refer once more to the statement made by the Minister of State for Finance in this House on March 25 of this year when she said, after the $255 million bail-out, that this bank is now a viable bank, it will be profitable in the future, and we will be repaid, as will other members of the support group, out of the future profits of the bank. That is the only thing that is unique. It was the failure of the Government to manage this situation properly and the misleading of the Canadian public and depositors who were induced to keep their deposits in the CCB.
I would like to draw attention to a telephone call we received from a gentleman who had purchased a $10,000 annuity five years ago at the Continental Trust Company. The company's accounts were frozen last June and on September 20 a liquidation was announced. Because his funds were not to be repaid within five years or less, they were not insured by the CDIC. The gentleman in question said that he would be happy to accept this, or not happy but he would accept it, probably reluctantly. He understood the terms under which he entered into this contract but he believed all Canadians were being treated the same way. Well, when he hears that uninsured depositors are being bailed out of two banks just two weeks after the Continental folded, how can he regard that as being
fair and equitable? Do you suppose that that gentleman regards the circumstances of the Canadian Commercial Bank or the Northland Bank as unique and justifying that kind of treatment? I suggest not.
This speech-if I may refer to the second canard-tells us that depositors who stayed with these banks shared the Government's view that regional financial institutions can play an important role in Canada. That is why the depositors stayed with the bank and that is why we are being told that these depositors are to be bailed out. That statement is so fatuous that it should not be uttered in this House. No Canadian is going to believe that depositors stayed with this bank because they were concerned about regional banks. They were concerned about their money and they were told by the Minister in this House that their money was safe.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, do you think that the City of Kanata, which I understand has some $7 million in one of these banks, left its money in the bank because it shared the Government's view that these regional financial institutions can play an important role? Do you think that the City of St. Catharines, Ontario, with $25 million of its taxpayers' money, did that as well? Does anyone suggest that the City of Westmount in my riding, with $2 million in the Northland Bank, left its money in on that belief? Surely this is the most extravagant canard that we have heard uttered in the House. These depositors left their money in that bank because they were told that their money was secure and that the bank was viable. Some of the shareholders may have stayed with these banks for the reasons suggested by the Minister, but the shareholders are not going to be reimbursed. Some of the debenture holders, but not all of them, may have stayed for those reasons as well. I will come to them in as few moments.
A third canard which will not fly is the statement by the Minister that our Government examined all the options at the time of the support package. I cannot say that that statement is untrue, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the options were examined, but the only sensible options were rejected and the option which was accepted was the worst of all possible worlds. Many of those options were described in some detail in the speech of my Leader yesterday. It is clear that the Minister was aware of the circumstances of the bank when she was first briefed in September 1984. There was a panic in March. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, the three great show biz events presented by the Government. The first was the First Ministers' Conference on St. Valentine's Day, then came the Shamrock Conference on St. Patrick's Day, and then the National Economic Summit on March 22. Right in the middle of that conference this financial Titanic, the CCB, struck an iceberg and started to sink.
No one was on the lookout, Mr. Speaker. The damage to the bank at that point was clearly beyond repair and it was inevitable that the CCB would go down. We were all invited to help bail it out and we did, being told that it was sound and would float. Speaking of options, Mr. Speaker, the chartered
October 8, 1985

banks even offered to examine the loan portfolio of the CCB to see if the bank really could float. That offer was denied. They also suggested that the management of the bank be changed because management was clearly at the root of the difficulties of the CCB. That suggestion was also rejected. When one suggests that the various options were examined, they may have been, but it is equally true that they were rejected. The bank immediately began to sink and the bail-out of $225 million was put right down a black hole on the strength of the Minister's recommendations. Worse than that, Mr. Speaker, they tied the Northland Bank to this financial Titanic and sent them both down. That could probably have been avoided by giving the Northland Bank a support package in March and allowing the CCB to go the way it was inevitably destined to
go-
We lost $225 million the first time around. We are now being asked for a further $875 million to pay off uninsured depositors. I see that Richardson Greenshields has estimated that the total loss will probably be in the neighbourhood of $2 billion. Do you know what $2 billion means, Mr. Speaker? It means that by the end of this exercise each Canadian taxpayer, of which, according to the 1982 tax returns filed, there are between 10 million and 11 million in Canada, will be required to fork up just under $200 in order to bail out the Minister and this Government from the disastrous course it set last March when it designed that support package for the CCB without knowing the facts. I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that each taxpayer can find better things to do with close to $200 of capital than to use it to pay off depositors and to bail out the Government from circumstances of its own making. To add insult to injury, we are all being asked to reach into our pockets and, blindfolded, hand that money over to depositors who present themselves for payment.
This brings me to the last canard. In his speech the Minister defends this on the ground of confidentiality. She says that to violate the confidentiality of the Bank Act would put all depositors in Canadian institutions at peril should any Government in future wish to get access to and publish that data. I heard the Member for Calgary South compound that canard by asking how you would like to have all of your financial data exposed in public. Nobody is asking for that, Mr. Speaker. [Translation]
All we want to know is who are the people who will receive this generous contribution from the Canadian taxpayers? Is that asking too much? The people do not even have to identify themselves to get this free payment. I, for one, find it absolutely unbelievable that we would be asked and even forced to do that through legislation in the House. If we keep going down the path already staked out by the Minister we will be forced to hand out our savings and our money to those nameless individuals. It is quite unthinkable. It is unacceptable. [English]
That is the reason that no sensible person could support this particular piece of legislation. How could we support this largess? This is not a case of people going to get their deposits
Depositors Compensation
from a bank under the provisions of the Bank Act. These people are having an ex gratia payment made to them by the taxpayers of this country. The amount of $875 billion which is being asked for here would require between $83 and $84 from every single taxpayer. That is not rational and does not even meet a test of common sense. That canard about confidentiality must be shot down as quickly as possible before it gets into flight.
I hope that Members of the Government side will have the courage to stand on this point and to say in caucus and to the Minister in question that this is not reasonable, fair, or sensible, that they will not accept it, and that they want an amendment to this Bill which will require any depositor who is to receive payment to be identified.

As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, we have four canards that cannot fly in these circumstances, and it is simply a matter of being reasonable, having a full explanation in the House, and a Government willing to accept the proposed amendment. Indeed, given the circumstances, we must support the motion because the Government has yet to take a reasonable position.

Therefore, I say that this Bill either has to go back to the drawing board or be radically amended. That is the reason I stand here to speak in support of a motion which was put to the House by our Leader yesterday.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had the benefit of the remarks of my hon. friend who was a member of the Cabinet during the infamous period of the National Energy Policy which is really the reason why we have had to take these steps on behalf of these western regional banks.
While I do not want to ask him to apologize for that, I would ask him to enlighten us on any efforts that were made by the former Liberal administration to tighten up the regulatory process. The Hon. Member will know that the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance chaired a committee which recommended in 1982, some three years ago, tightening the regulatory process for banks. He will know that nothing was done, despite the fact that it was well known in financial circles that much had to be done to improve the regulatory process.
As well as having to bear the shame for the National Energy Program, the Hon. Member must bear the shame for the fact that during the time he was a member of Cabinet no action was taken by the Liberal Party to tighten the regulatory process. Although this is a rather large confessional in which to make such a statement, having seen all of the evidence and facing this embarrassment, will he not do the honourable thing and admit that during the last five years when he was a member of Cabinet the very important regulatory process was left to further ruin and ultimately led to the failure of these banks? I invite him to do the honourable thing at this time.

October 8, 1985
Depositors Compensation

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is speaking tongue in cheek, which is fair enough in the course of this debate. I would suggest to him that regulations can always be improved, but no banks failed while I was in Government. I suspect the reason was that whereas the regulatory mechanism might not have been as good as it should have been, the Ministers were on top of their Departments and knew what was taking place. This kind of problem would not have escaped their attention. That is a reasonable assumption to make.
However, that is not to say that the regulatory apparatus should not be improved. In fact, with the group of Ministers in Government today I suggest that the regulatory mechanisms should be tightened substantially in all departments to ensure that when those Ministers are not at the controls and do not know what is going on the bureaucracy can keep the ship of state on course.
With respect to the national energy question, I would have thought that the Hon. Member might have been one of those to stand in his place and admit that there was a monumental gaffe created and that the National Energy Program has become a whipping boy for every problem that emerges in western Canada. For Members of the Government, the National Energy Program has become the motto "Damn the CPR", recalling the old saying out West. However, before this debate became more partisan as the magnitude of this financial Titanic revealed itself, the Minister of State for Finance put the position clearly in the House. On March 25 in the House she said, speaking of the CCB, that this particular problem was triggered by something that happened within the bank's loan portfolio in California which then, of course, created problems within the organization as a whole.
That was an honest statement. That was taking the high road. I suspect that she received a call from the Prime Minister's office and subsequently I have noted that she too has leaned to the pressure to blame everything on the National Energy Program.
I believe that the Minister told us exactly as it was and is. I repeat that our Government had no bank failures and indeed the present Government probably requires a better regulatory mechanism if this kind of disaster is not to repeat itself.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I wish to thank Members of the House for giving unanimous consent to allow me to make my remarks in my place this afternoon. I understand that from the television angle I look like a midget. I assure the people of Canada that I am not. I wish to especially thank the Government Member who allowed me to make my remarks this afternoon. Tomorrow, hopefully, a cast will be put on my foot but it will lay me up for the next 72 hours.
There are some very important questions I wish to address in the course of this deabte. They go beyond a partisan approach. Bank failures and the possibility of bank failures is a serious question that we have not had to address in this country for many years. We have always assumed that our bank system was safe and sound. Over the years, Canadians have taken pride in the security of our banking system. This supposition on the part of depositors and the public of Canada, as well as Governments of all political persuasions, perhaps lulled us into a false sense of security.
Although the events of the last year have shocked all of us, I believe it should not have been a shock because the warning signs were there. We have seen a significant number of smaller financial institutions, namely trust companies, go under in the last number of years. Therefore, I dispute the statement made by the Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), a former Minister of Finance. While he is technically correct that no bank went under when he was Minister of Finance, it is true that a number of smaller trust companies failed when his party was in power.
There had been many warning signals that our financial institutions were in trouble and the fact that some have failed warants increased regulation and support for CDIC and the office of the Inspector General of Banks. I believe that it is also true that the Inspector General of Banks requested more manpower in the past and that this was turned down by Treasury Board under the previous administration. It must accept responsibility for the sad state of affairs we are facing today.
I do not envy the position in which the Government finds itself. While the two banks in question are not among the large banks in this country, they are important as far as banks in the world are concerned. A significant number of small businesses, particularly in Calgary and Edmonton, had their funds tied up in this institution. I appreciate the difficulty in which the Government finds itself. No Government wants to see a large number of small companies and small business people going under through no fault of their own. We know as well that there is a fair number of those depositors who are not sophis-
October 8, 1985

ticated depositors in the true sense of the word. Many of them are charitable organizations and public institutions such as municipalities, hospitals, et cetera. While we oppose the Bill, we are not adverse to helping such individuals, as well as public and quasi-public charitable institutions. My colleague, our finance critic, suggested the establishment of a special fund for hardship cases. Perhaps we should consider assisting small businesses which use banking institutions, not for the interest paid but for the services offered, such as chequing accounts and so on. Perhaps they should be given 100 per cent on their deposits.
Obviously the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank situation points out that we desperately need some policies. Is the Government to become the backer or the guarantor of last resort in every instance or in every case? If that is the case, it puts the country or the public purse in an impossible situation.
When does a Government bail out uninsured depositors and when does it not do so? It is an impossible situation. Surely we cannot bail out only the big guys and not the small guys. That is inherently unfair. During Question Period today we learned that no other Government of any country has bailed out uninsured depositors. Uninsured depositors have been bailed out, but it is the financial system or the banking system which has paid. When the Government considers options in developing a consistent policy, it has to keep the principle in mind that the financial system must cover the cost of any bail-out of uninsured depositors, not the public purse. That is one principle upon which we must insist.
After all, if the Government has to bail out uninsured depositors in the end from the public purse, we in the New Democratic Party suggest that it is about time it collected some of the profits to be made. Why should the Government pick up the losses but never have an opportunity to participate in the profits? Perhaps there should be an available fund so that credit unions, municipalities and hospital boards with excess funds for a small period of time can invest in a publicly owned and controlled deposit-like institution and not experience the risks which they obviously experienced with Northland and the Canadian Commercial Bank. To reiterate the point, if the Government is to pick up all losses, surely in heaven's name it should also have an opportunity to participate in the profit-making.
The other point to which I wanted to address myself has been addressed by a fair number of Government Members, particularly those from Alberta. They made the point in the House that the cause of the problem was the National Energy Program. I was not happy with the National Energy Program for a variety of reasons, most of which were quite different from those of the Conservative Party when it was in Opposition. However, I also felt that in many ways the NEP was a grab by the central Government of the resources of western Canada. As a western Canadian, I was not all that happy with the program. However, to blame the collapse of the CCB and
Depositors Compensation
the Northland Bank on the National Energy Program alone is a disservice to western Canada. Government Members, particularly those from Alberta, must recognize a few simple facts. The economic atmosphere which existed in Alberta during the oil boom was very unhealthy. The land speculation which was occurring, particularly in the cities of Edmonton and Calgary, was also unhealthy. The Province of Saskatchewan experienced a bit of a boom during that period of time, but it had a NDP Government which believed in economic planning and in Keynesian economics. Essentially it believed that in boom times some of the excess wealth should be put away for rainy days. The Government of Saskatchewan at that time did not allow the land speculation which occurred in Edmonton and in Calgary. Through the Saskatchwan Housing Corporation, that Government became involved in developing new tracts of land so that the prices of homes in Regina did not go sky-high. In that way the cost of housing and urban land in Regina was kept down, so that when the boom started to fade that province did not experience the type of bust which occurred in Edmonton and in Calgary. It was able to maintain a stable and sound economic climate in the Province of Saskatchewan. Unfortunately, in Alberta, with a gung-ho type of free enterprise system, huge profits were made when the time was ripe, but when the bust came, all the costs and social hardships ensued which are very often borne by the public.
It is ironic that these great free enterprisers from Alberta are now standing in the House, justifying a Government bailout and insisting upon more Government regulations and inspectors. What a contradiction in terms, especially coming from those gung-ho free enterprisers out of Alberta.
The type of political atmosphere which has existed in Alberta has not been a healthy one. It has not been healthy for the country and certainly not for the Province of Alberta. The people of that province are now paying the price. Hopefully they will understand some of the political repercussions and implications of what happened. The period of time during the Alberta boom was a period in which banks and business people became greedy. They tried to increase their profits as much as they could. Their greed led to the downfall of the Canadian Commercial Bank. It is unfortunate when I hear members of the Conservative Party from Alberta indicate in the House that they have not learned that lesson. They do not attribute any of the downfall of the CCB to the bad management, the high risk loans and the type of greed which prevailed in that province at that particular time. It was that greed which led to the downfall of the Canadian Commercial Bank and of the Northland Bank. That greed was abetted by the Government of Alberta and its political philosophy or attitude which allowed a tremendous boom to occur but, when the bust occurred, which led to many shattered lives and businesses. It is a prime example of how a responsible Government involved in economic planning would have taken a different course, as we did in the Province of Saskatchewan. Yes, we had a boom, but we did not have a boom based upon greed. We did not allow the greed to send the prices of real estate sky-high. When the bad times came we had a cushion. Surely the people

of Alberta, as other western Canadians who have experienced the boom and bust cycle, should have known better.

Mr. Speaker, I want to first thank my colleagues in the House for giving me unanimous consent to add
the word "dependants" because the way the original motion ran it was rather redundant. As we know all members of the Canadian Armed Forces have dental and medical plans.
It has become an issue in this past while, Mr. Speaker, particularly among dependants of the Armed Forces personnel, that they do not have access to private plans as do most others in the workforce in Canada. For example, teachers in most jurisdictions have access to a group dental plan and are able to purchase or insure their families and their children for the required dental care by joining the plans. The cost is not prohibitive. It runs approximately $15 to $20 per month.
People who have made representations to me have indicated very clearly that they are not asking the Government to pick up the tab. What they are asking the Government to do is establish a group for them, approach an insurance company on their behalf as a group so that individuals within the Armed Forces may subscribe to that by way of payroll deduction. In other words, they are not asking the Government to add to the budget of any department; they are not asking the Government to do one single thing except establish a group so that dependants of Armed Forces personnel may, by their husbands or wives payroll deductions, enrol in the dental plan. In this day and age I think we all know the difficulty and the cost of medical services and how they have gone up dramatically. In this day and age it is not uncommon to find companies that employ 37, 40 and 50 people enrolled in a dental plan on behalf of their employees. I just cite a couple of examples. There is a small school board in my riding in northeastern Alberta that has 211 families enrolled and 126 singles. They are all teachers and they are enrolled in a dental plan. The cost for the singles is around $14 a month and for the families around $35 a month. The key was that the insurance company that was approached had to have a unit to work with and this they do not have in the Armed Forces at the present time.
Another small company has 37 singles enrolled at a cost of $15 a month and 16 families at $39 a month, or slightly higher depending on the make-up of the family. TransCanada Pipelines is another much larger one. I will not quote the cost but because of its size it is significantly lower than the ones 1 indicated before. They have 1,480 families and 414 singles enrolled in their plan.
One can easily determine by looking at all of the Armed Forces personnel across Canada whose dependants are not covered by any dental services that it would make a very large group indeed. I think it would be very lucrative for an insurance company and many insurance companies would come forward and be quite willing to cover a plan like this if it was administered at the payroll deduction centre. Queens regulations today indicate that there is an entitlement to dental treatment. Of course all members of the Armed Forces personnel office are men. Dental care for dependants under certain circumstances does exist, for instance, in an isolated or an overseas posting. In some isolated units such as Alsask, Saskatchewan; Goose Bay, Gypsumville, Manitoba; Holberg, B.C.; Inuvik; Masset, B.C.; Mont Apica, Quebec; Senneterre, Quebec; Sioux Lookout, Ontario; and Yellowknife, NWT
October 8, 1985

dental facilities are covered along with medical, for obvious reasons.
Cold Lake, a major base in my riding, was considered isolated to March 1, 1983. One can imagine the problems that existed when on March 1, 1983 Cold Lake base, which houses approximately 4,000 dependants living on the base, all of a sudden was without dental coverage. There were cases where some of the children were having orthodontic work done and they were not prepared for the bill which came in for the cost of their dental care. They were not able to get the necessary insurance coverage. There are cases documented to be by constituents where individuals, families, mothers had to leave the home where they were working and raising their children and get a job to pay a dental bill. Somehow this just does not ring properly to me. I think there is something wrong when the Department of National Defence or Treasury Board will not take the time to just set up or set in motion and set in place an organization that would allow individuals at their request to come forward and say "deduct from my monthly pay for enrollment into the dental plan". They do not ask for something for nothing. They are willing to pay for it.
I am not going to waste the time of the House on this. 1 think I have made myself clear. I am not asking the Government to put forward any money. I am only making a reasonable request to the Government to set up a group plan to allow members of the Armed Forces to participate in a payroll deduction plan so that their families can be protected with dental care.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADIAN ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise in support of the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) and his motion which would provide for dental care plan for dependants of Armed Forces personnel. I am glad to support this. I am sure that there is no Member of the House who would want to oppose it. Certainly no one will want to oppose it vocally. I only hope that the Members of his own Party will support it actively by allowing this motion to come to a vote so that the House can declare itself in support of this very important motion.
I think that all Members in the House will agree that the Conservative Government has taken a bit of a beating in the last few weeks. The Hon. Member's motion gives it an opportunity to redeem itself in the eyes of the Canadian public. I commend this not only to the back-benchers but also to members of the Government. Here is the chance for the Government to take a positive, assertive role in helping to do something for the Canadian people.
I think we must recognize that the failure to include dental care in our comprehensive medicare program is something that needs to be addressed. We need dental care for more than just Armed Forces personnel, but that is a good place to begin. Back in 1964 when Chief Justice Emmett Hall drafted the report that led to medicare, he said that we had to go beyond
Canadian Armed Forces
simply paying for visits to the doctor. In his report, he said the following:
No one would suggest that the payment of medical bills is not an important item, but it is after all but one item in the full range of health services and in any objective approach it could not be permitted to dominate the whole field.
There are many other areas in the health service field that cry out for improvement: mental illness, retarded children, crippled children, the crippling diseases, paraplegics, the aged and infirm, dental services and drug costs.
We have not really begun to move on the basic agenda contained in Mr. Justice Emmett Hall's report. I think it is time that we did so. We should not only look at the need for dental care for Armed Forces personnel but we should move toward a comprehensive dental care program for Canadians all across the country.
It is important to realize the the need for dental care, and I would like to share with the House a few statistics regarding that need. Only 50 per cent of Canadians visit dentists annually. The fact is that children from low-income families are three times as likely to have poor teeth as those from other families. In 1979 in Ontario, 29 per cent of decayed teeth in five-year olds had not been filled. By the age of 13, 32 per cent of decayed teeth in children had not been filled. This indicates that there is a very large segment of society that is not getting even the most basic of dental care. In fact, pregnant women also tend to have poor teeth. A decade-old study done by Nutrition Canada indicated that 90 per cent of pregnant women under the age of 20 had bad teeth.
While most provinces offer some kind of denticare program, it is significant that the Provinces of Ontario and British Columbia, two of the provinces which should be among the richest Provinces of Canada, do not offer those programs. The Province of British Columbia was beginning to establish such a program when it was cut back in the name of false restraint. To restrain public spending at the expense of the dental health of children is, in my opinion, a crime.
The failure to provide adequate dental care along with our medicare program indicates that we still consider dental care to be somewhat of a fringe benefit or cosmetic option that can be taken or left alone. The feeling is that if people can afford dental care, that is fine, but if they are too poor to afford it, it is not that serious. This is a fundamental mistake. Unless there is an active program of dental care, people will pay for it with their health in later years. The emphasis should be on early detection and prevention. Healthy teeth and gums are not simply a matter of looking good but are a matter of basic health.
From my own family experience, and I am sure from the family experiences of Members on all sides of the House, I know that even orthodontic work is not simply a cosmetic matter. The need to have a healthy bite and proper spacing is something that affects basic health. Yet we know how terribly expensive orthodontic work can be. Many Members of this House wish that we were covered by some kind of a dental program to meet those needs. If this is true for Members of Parliament who have a reasonable salary, to put it in terms my fellow Members will appreciate, and if we find it difficult to pay for orthodontic work, how much more is that the case for

October 8, 1985
Canadian Armed Forces
other Canadians, many of whom are on very restricted incomes? Certainly that applies to the vast number of people in the Armed Forces.
We know that many unions have negotiated dental plans for their members and members' families. However, a very high percentage of Canadians are still not covered by any dental program, and that includes members of the Armed Forces and public servants. When other Canadians are able to negotiate programs with their employers, why is it that the Canadian Government is such a poor employer?
I am very happy to suggest that this Bill is a good beginning. Let us begin with the Armed Forces. Give the Armed Forces the opportunity to negotiate a dental plan. Let us then extend this opportunity to all federal public employees and let us work toward the day when there is a comprehensive dental program that will service the needs of all Canadians.
On that basis, I am very pleased to support the motion of the Hon. Member and I hope that it will come to a vote. 1 know that if it does come to a vote, it will receive the unanimous support of all Members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for bringing this motion before the House today. The motion refers to Canadian Armed Forces personnel. I understand that that was an error and that the Hon. Member means to refer to dependants of military personnel. That is a very good point indeed.
We must remember that members of the Canadian Armed Forces are consistently on the move. We know that they do not have the opportunity to settle in and form deep roots in the communities to which they are posted.
