speechtext:
The Hon. Member wants to throw in a joke, but this is no joking matter. As I was saying, members of the Armed Forces are posted from place to place and each time they go to a different base, they have to find a dentist in the area who will look after their dependants. Then, two years later, they may be posted to another base and they have to go through the same process all over again.
The Canadian Armed Forces personnel themselves have had a dental plan for some time. The "Dental Treatment and Service for Dependants and other Civilians" document dealing with this matter contains one paragraph of particular interest here and is with regard to dental examination prior to posting to isolated areas. It reads as follows:
Service members, dependants and other civilians may be located in an area where limited or no dental care is available. Prior to their departure and to ensure that they do not become an administrative burden, they will be provided with a dental examination, advised of their dental condition and of the dental care restrictions at the new location.
I believe that that is a very important provision. I share with my hon. colleagues a great admiration for all members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the important work they carry out for this nation. My Party and I feel that it is important to
make every effort to ensure that our military personnel and their dependants receive every service to make their lives more enjoyable and, indeed, more comfortable. Theirs is a task which requires a great sacrifice. This is the least we can do as a nation and as a Government to show our appreciation for their dedicated service. Therefore, I support the general thrust of the motion which seeks to make available to dependants of Armed Forces personnel an adequate dental plan.
[DOT] (W20)
I would also like to place on the record that it is not only in cases of medical care and dental care that the dependants of Armed Forces personnel have a challenge as they move from place to place in Canada. I had the privilege of teaching in an Armed Forces high school. We had families coming and going all the time. It is very difficult for families, children and teenagers to adjust in moving from one community to another and in changing friends and schools. I think we need to have an appreciation for the other pressures and challenges which families of military personnel face. Therefore it is incumbent upon the House to look very seriously upon this motion which is before us today.
I can understand that there has been an expression of willingness on the part of the dependants who would benefit from such a plan to underwrite the costs of it to a degree. I can think of no reason to oppose such a plan. I think it is an admirable one, especially if there will be no additional drain on the federal Treasury other than through the matching of funds which are put in by dependants of military personnel. It would be a good plan for the Department of National Defence to sit down with the Department of National Health and Welfare and, indeed, with the Health Ministers from the various provinces to discuss how such plans can indeed be put into place.
While we are discussing dental plans for dependants of Armed Forces personnel, we certainly cannot overlook the fact that we have a great many civilians in Canada who are in dire need of dental care. Last week an individual who needs new dentures came into my office. He is an elderly person and cannot afford the $650 which it will set him back to pay for those dentures. There is no question that while we look upon a dental plan for dependants of the Canadian Armed Forces that we certainly must be looking at this situation across the nation as a whole. My hon. friend across the way who made the comment earlier spoke about root canals. I did not understand what he was saying in the first instance. However, I appreciate his comments in view of the statement I was making at the time.
There is a good feeling in the House with respect to the motion before us. I think there would be a good feeling in the House to look at dental plans across the nation as a whole. We citizens realize that when we have these plans someone has to pay for them. The money has to come from somewhere. I think it behooves each one of us, each and every Canadian, to realize that if we are to have this type of coverage then it would be in a contibutory fashion. The taxpayers would come in with a
October 8, 1985

share of the cost, as would the provinces at the federal-provincial health level.
Canadians are fortunate to have the types of medical care plans which are in place in Canada already. With the wealth of our resources and with the human generosity which Canadians have shown with respect to looking after their neighbours and in being their brothers' keepers, there is a feeling that there are many people in Canada today who just simply cannot afford the costs of dental care. This is a very serious issue indeed. We should look at it and try to make progress in order to help these people out in the future.
I assure all interested parties that given the nature of this Government I doubt if there will be any real action taken with respect to this plan being implemented in the foreseable future. We have seen that this Government has been cutting back in many areas with respect to taxes and pension allocations relating to individual Canadians. That is no reason for it not to look at improvements and, indeed, even review the cut-backs which have taken place which affect individual Canadians. We cannot continue to cut back on personal benefits to the general public of Canada and still end up 10 years down the road with the good quality of service we have today in medical care.
It takes a great deal of diplomacy to bring about dental plans and medical care plans because they involve federal-provincial relations to thenth degree. The provincial Governments in Canada are always trying to get as much money out of the federal Treasury as they possibly can while the federal Treasury always tries to hold back as much as it can. The federal Government does not want to raise taxes which places it in the bad eye of the public. I suggest to the Hon. Member who puts forward the motion today that he has many friends who support his cause. I hope the Government is prepared to take a serious approach with respect to the implementation of a dental care plan for dependants of members of the Canadian Armed Forces and at the same time look at a national dental care plan for Canada.
As we progress as a nation, broaden our industrial base and manage our national resources better than they have ever been managed at times in the past, we will be in a better position to pay for these services. We will be in a better position to pay the Government portion for the service while at the same time retaining the medical care services which are already in place in Canada. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of National Defence and the Dental Association of Canada should have a very close relationship in order to overcome many of the difficulties faced by the families of our Armed Forces as a result of being moved from community to community. I would hope that all dentists across Canada would be particularly sensitive to the needs of new people moving into Canadian Armed Forces bases in Canada and that they would take those people into their offices and treat them as first-class customers while they are in the community. It is very important that we make these families feel welcome wherever they go in Canada. Of course, one of the ways of making them feel welcome is to make sure the community to which they are moved or posted has the necessary services to provide to them.

In the case where these families are moved to an isolated community, I quoted the section from the DND document which explains the kinds of services which are available to them before they leave.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would simply say that the Liberal Party of Canada is very much in favour of looking into a dental plan for dependants of the Canadian Armed Forces personnel. Certainly, at the same time, we are in favour of looking at the national picture for other Canadians across this country who need that type of attention.

I do not believe there is anyone in this House who would disagree that the Armed Forces are entitled to expect fair and equitable treatment as part of the terms and conditions under which they render service to this country.
It may be useful, to put this debate into context, Mr. Speaker, to describe to the House the general practice followed in establishing military compensation. It is essentially based on compatibility with the Public Service. This principle was established by a decision of Cabinet-I might say, a Liberal Cabinet-in October of 1971. It was reaffirmed in 1982 by the then President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of National Defence. I might remind my hon. friend that he was in the House at that time on the Government side and supported that decision.
Although military compensation is based on comparability with the Public Service, it cannot be equated precisely because there are many functions performed in the military context which do not exist in the Public Service. I believe we all agree with that. To bridge those differences, a large number of Public Service trades have been taken as standards, for pay purposes, for certain military trades. By using averaging process and projections, it is possible to arrive at a basis upon which the Treasury Board can establish military compensation on the recommendations of the Department of National Defence. This process has its good side and its bad side. I am the first to admit that. However, I believe that it is fact to say that over the years it has resulted in a compensation package which is comprehensive in its scope and is indeed fair and equitable to members of the Armed Forces as well as to their dependants.
I feel, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, that I should take this occasion to review some of the programs which are in place to provide for their welfare. First and foremost is their pension plan which ranks among the best in the country. Members of the Armed Forces have an insurance plan to protect their incomes in the event of long-term disability. The
Government contributes to the cost of providing provincial health insurance for their dependants and makes available a program to cover the dependants for health costs which are not provincially insured. Members of the Armed Forces have a sound program to provide benefits for injury or death on duty, a cost-shared life insurance program and an extensive program of income supplementation which ensures the maintenance of a decent standard of living for his dependants in the event of death or disability of a member from any cause.
There are measures for the continuance of pay during a short-term illness and comprehensive programs of medical and dental services at government expense. I am not citing these few examples to suggest that members of the Armed Forces are over-protected. The programs in place are no more than are due those members in comparison with other groups and by the special nature of their duties. The purpose of giving these examples is to simply illustrate that the Armed Forces are in no sense a forgotten group in terms of their service-related benefits, nor will it ever be a forgotten group under this administration.
With that background in mind, I wish to address some of the broader issues which the Treasury Board must consider when group benefit programs of this kind are under discussion.
Treasury Board is directly responsible for the expenditure of public funds on group benefits not only for the Armed Forces but for the Public Service, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and many other groups as well; consequently, the Board cannot view a proposed change to the compensation package of any one of these groups in total isolation, but must consider the implications for all of the groups. This does not mean that a change in the benefits of one group will automatically apply to the others. Such is quite definitely not the case, because otherwise the individuality so essential to each of the groups would be lost. The ability of the employer to tailor benefits to the needs of unique groups would be seriously undermined. If that were the case, the possibility always exists that benefits which would be appropriate for one group would be applied inappropriately to another.
I said at the outset that members of the Armed Forces must be treated fairly and equitably. By the same token, employees in the Public Service and members of the RCMP must be treated fairly and equitably. Again, this does not mean that benefits must be the same for all three groups. Service in the Armed Forces and employment in the Public Service are different in many obvious ways and those differences are reflected in various ways. For example. Armed Forces members have access to a program of comprehensive dental care which is paid for by the Government.
In view of the fact that there have been discussions with union representatives concerning employees who do not benefit from a Government sponsored dental plan, it may be of interest to all Hon. Members if I were to outline recent developments in the ongoing discussions which have been
October 8, 1985

taking place with Public Service unions on the dental care issue.
All Hon. Members will be aware that Public Service unions have been seeking a dental plan for a number of years, and their position has been clearly stated. Succeeding Governments have undertaken to try to ensure that public servants enjoy a compensation package which is comparable to the package in other employment sectors. That philosophy is much easier to expound that to apply. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that a goodly number of working Canadians do not have dental plans to help them with their expenses, and we should not lose sight of that fact. Nevertheless, when one examines those groups of employers which have traditionally been used as the basis for com-parision, dental plans are indeed widespread.
It is important to recognize that the introduction of a dental plan will have an impact on the Government's benefit expenditures. All Hon. Members will appreciate this when I point out that, if all three groups-the Public Service and dependants of members of the Armed Forces and the RCMP-were covered by dental care plans, the potential insured population, including the families, could be well over one million persons. The actual number of plan members, if the plan were universal, would exceed 300,000. Simply for illustration, the total cost could exceed $100 million annually for a very basic plan. Now, Mr. Speaker, the Government would not pick up this entire cost, but only a share of it. Nevertheless, the potential expenditure of public funds is considerable.
It is only natural that the unions want to see a dental plan introduced on the most favourable possible terms for their members. For its part, the Government must seek the best achievable balance between its responsibility to provide a competitive benefit package and its responsibility to taxpayers to keep its over-all expenditures on Public Service benefits at at reasonable and defensible level.
This Government approached the issue in good faith. Serious negotiations were undertaken with unions in short order, and real impetus was given to the issue for the first time. These negotiations are still under way and the Government has every intention of pursuing them to a fair and responsible conclusion. Naturally there can be no guarantee of an early conclusion to the negotiations, nor can the spirit of the negotiations be betrayed by discussing the details publicly at this time. However, I am confident that they are being pursued with vigour.
We have remarked at some length on the discussions with Public Service unions. The reason I have done so is to demonstrate this Government's commitment to find a way to extend dental care to those groups which wish to have it, where it can be demonstrated that it is possible to do so, and it is warranted to do so, on the basis of comparability. At the same time, this must be achieved in a fiscally responsible way at a time when so many demands are being made, by competing priorities, on the finite resource available to the Government.
In closing, having gone through some oral surgery recently, I know the expense is large. At the same time, dentists tell me that with the new methods of teeth care and education, the

The House will know that we have put these negotiations on a new footing. Instead of using the technique of the former Government of shouting and threatening, we are sitting down at the bargaining table and discussing the issues between employer and employee on a very reasonable and meaningful basis.
One of the things referred to is the question of a dental plan for all public servants. I am pleased to tell the House that

October 8, 1985
Canadian Armed Forces
those matters are going forward. There is no question that the cost of dental services concerns every Member of this House, whether on behalf of himself or herself or of dependants. It is a very major cost in today's society. I know that in Ontario fluoridation, although it was resisted quite strongly originally, has improved the teeth of the people who have had the benefit of it. I know for a fact that my children do not seem to go to the dentist nearly as often as I used to.
However, I have had some experience with orthodontists. As a result, I want my five children to be orthodontists because I think there is a great future for young people in that profession. I do not know whether one should refer to personal experiences, but last week my daughter had her braces removed after having worn them for some 18 months. Orthodontists do some wonderful work. Her teeth were straight and she was looking forward to going to a party the next day. I think that everyone's children should have that advantage and that is certainly on the table at the present time although I am not at liberty to say what point those negotiations have reached.
Having set the stage with those general remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the Government's position with respect to a dental plan. I know that Members of the House are anxious to have a hard look taken at a dental plan for all people who work under federal jurisdiction. Members of the Armed Forces and all other public servants are well aware that for many other Canadians in the work force dental bills are not the problem they used to be because these employees have access, through their employers, to dental plans which pay their dental bills. It is bound to be a source of concern for members of the Armed Forces that they not only have access to dental services, but are able to pay for them. In referring to the problems of the Armed Forces my colleague made reference to physical access in that dental facilities are not available in all of the places where Armed Forces personnel are posted. We want to have that matter up-graded. At the same time as we are concerned about the physical access we must be concerned about financial access. There are dental facilities available to armed services employees at cost. We want to have that expanded.
I would like to put the entire question of a dental plan in greater perspective. I think it is fair to say that the dental plan for public servants is seen as what might be called a capping stone of an entire benefits package which the Government is working on at the present time. We know that it has become the norm among large employers and the federal Government, as a very large employer, must conform to what is being done in the non-public servant world. Many of these plans accept a large part of the responsibility for ensuring that employees have access to the programs that spread the risk, attract the employer funds, and promote the financial security of the employees who are retiring, who become ill, or who are injured on the job as well as the security of the employee's family in the event of his or her death.
I think it is fair to say that the Government of Canada has been a fair employee through the years. We would like to have an increase in that fairness in many ways and we would like to do that within the demands and constaints of the horrendous deficit that was left to us by the Liberal Party. We would do many things in terms of social benefits for all Canadians if we had not been left with the crippling deficit amassed by the Liberal Party over the last 16 years. That is a partisan view and I do not want it to interfere with a non-partisan discussion on the issue of a dental plan for dependants of armed services employees.
The Government is criticized if it is not seen to be spending taxpayers' money wisely. There is no question that to many people a dental plan put into place by the Government would be seen to be spending the money wisely. Sometimes we are damned if wo do and damned if we do not. For that reason we are taking a hard look at different types of dental plans and considering the cost. I am in a position to personally assure the House that we have discussed this matter with the interested parties and are studying it carefully to ensure that it is not only a fair plan for employees, but reasonable for the employer.
The Government has been concerned about the issues of pensions, long-term disability insurance, health insurance, and numerous other programs as well as being concerned about the question of a dental plan. The Government is ahead of the market in some ways in that it is doing more for its employees than is being done for those in private enterprise. In other areas, such as this one, we find the Government is lagging behind that which is the norm in private enterprise. It is our job to up-grade and yet not overtake such that we will be criticized by private enterprise which says that it cannot afford to do with the money it has left what the Government is trying to do with the money given it by private enterprise. That is a balancing act which all Governments have to do with public employees.
There is no question that the Government must promote dental hygiene, whether preventative methods or orthodontic work. There is no question that we are continuing the work of the previous Government with regard to promoting dental hygiene. No matter how critical I have been of the previous regime, and no matter how many opportunities it has given me, I have never been critical of its efforts with respect to dental hygiene. I would like to conclude on that point and perhaps continue the next time this matter is brought before the House.

Mr. Speaker, you may be aware of a very serious pollution and health problem in Metropolitan Toronto that has existed for many years. This problem has resulted in the closing of most of the beaches on the waterfront of Toronto along Lake Ontario in the last three or four summers, but it has existed for much longer. In any event, the beaches have been closed as a result of water pollution caused by raw sewage that has been flowing into Lake Ontario from the homes in Metropolitan Toronto. This has been caused by an antiquated sewer system in many parts of Metropolitan Toronto. It is a sewer system which combines both sanitary sewers with storm sewers. Of course, that means that the storm water created during a severe rain storm flows into the same sewer pipe into which sanitary sewage flows. When there is a storm, this overflows the filtration plants, floods into the rivers and streams and then pollutes the waterfront with raw sewage, causing not only a pollution problem but a severe health problem. That is particularly severe in the southern part of my riding which contains a major portion of the Borough of East York.
The problem is that the combined sewer system is antiquated. The problem can only be solved by separating the sanitary sewer system and the storm sewer system. This is being done in newer subdivisions in the newer urban areas but has not been done as yet in the older urban areas of cities because it is an extremely costly process. This problem not only results in lake pollution but in a health hazard in individual homes all over. When there is a rain storm in my riding, the combined water in the sewer pipes-some of it sanitary, some of it storm- backs up quite frequently into basements and floods those basements with raw sewage. It is quite clear that this creates an obvious health hazard.
As I said, the solution is to separate these two storm sewers, which is a costly process. The municipalities in Metropolitan Toronto have committed large sums-in fact millions of dollars-for a great many years toward separating their sewer system. The Province of Ontario has assisted in many instances as well and has provided millions of dollars.
Metropolitan Toronto, particularly a portion of my riding which includes the Borough of East York, has been looking for federal funding for a number of years. Between 1962 and 1982 we received federal funding for sewer separation problems. Unfortunately that has disappeared since 1982. The federal Government did supply funding for sewer separation programs as part of its job creation program, and I must give the former
Adjournment Debate
Government a great deal of credit for that, but once this funding expires, it has been made clear that there will be no extension of that program.
We need and are looking for further federal assistance in the sewer separation problem in order to eliminate pollution and the health hazard involved. I was pleased to see that last week, the National Water Policy Report recommended that there be some additional funding from the federal Government for both the municipalities and the provinces to help eliminate this problem.
Yesterday, I put a question on this subject to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), asking whether he supported the recommendations contained in the National Water Policy Report or the Pearse report, and whether he would urge the Government to contribute financially to help with local sewer improvement programs. In fact, the Minister indicated that he had met with his provincial counterparts and that they had discussed the problem and the report. There was an indication that the federal Government was prepared to consider it. As of yesterday we had an indication of hope from the Minister that some help and some support would be forthcoming. I trust that the Parliamentary Secretary this evening will be able to turn that hope into help, and give us an indication that the federal Government will agree to giving financial help for sewer improvement projects to the municipalities. I am looking forward to hearing from him in that respect.

subtopic: TRADE-CANADIAN LUMBER EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
TRADE-CANADIAN LUMBER EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I directed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) concerning Canadian lumber exports to the United States and the position of the Government of Canada.
By way of introduction, the whole issue of trade and trade-related matters is becoming of increasing importance to Canadians not only on the West Coast but indeed throughout Canada. Basically the thrust of my concern was that the United States Ambassador suggested in his speech in Saskatoon that Canadians in the lumber industry ought to voluntarily reduce the amount of their exports to the United States.
Some individuals in the United States Congress and others are concerned that Canada has increased relatively substantially the amount of lumber exported to the United States and as a conciliatory measure the United States suggests that we should voluntarily limit or restrict those lumber exports.
Many individuals in the industry certainly do not agree with the United States ambassador. I do not agree with what he has said and by his reply to my question the Minister has indicated as well that he does not agree with that statement. I had hoped to obtain from the Minister while questioning him, and perhaps I will now through the Parliamentary Secretary, exactly what has transpired between the Minister of State for External Affairs and the United States ambassador.
It is not sufficient, I suggest to you, that we just hear that the Minister does not agree. I think we have to know what was said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We have to know if a diplomatic note was forwarded, the form of those representations, and whether representations were made by the Prime Minister to the President with regard to this particular issue.
It does not suffice to say that this whole matter cannot be revealed because we are now in the process of opening up general prospects for the negotiation of free trade with the United States. There are just too many jobs on the West Coast, particularly in the Province of British Columbia where unemployment is extremely high at this point in time, for the Government to provide us with such a very short answer to this very, very important problem.
I can understand that if perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs has rebuked, if you will, the United States ambassador regarding this particular issue that perhaps he does not want to say so publicly. But I think in the Canadian interests, notwithstanding the Minister's own personal affection, if you will, for the United States ambassador, we have to know what Canadian policy is, what was said on behalf of Canadians, when it was said and where it was said. These issues are of paramount importance to Canadians.
I would hope that when the Parliamentary Secretary avails himself of this opportunity to reply in respect of my concerns he will shed light on this important matter. Canadians from coast to coast will be watching and listening to what he is going to be saying on behalf of all the people of Canada. I await with great interest the Parliamentary Secretary's remarks.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-CANADIAN LUMBER EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question. I too am very deeply concerned about jobs.
As the former Mayor of Dollard-Des Ormeaux and a long time active worker in my community I may tell him that in the City of St. Laurent there are 78,000 jobs and every time we see protectionist elements arising in the United States, we expect that those jobs will be affected.
The United States is the single most important market for Canadian lumber producers, taking 60 per cent of all Canadian production. There has been a flurry of congressional Bills aimed at restricting Canadian lumber imports, the most important of which is legislation introduced by Congressman Sam Gibbons. In short, the Gibbons' Bill would modify U.S. countervail law to deem that a subsidy existed where Canadian stumpage prices fell short of an arbitrary U.S. benchmark.
While we continue to focus our representations on the Congress and Administration in Washington we have, since the outset, developed a comprehensive and well co-ordinated campaign of private and public diplomacy to meet this threat to continued access for Canadian softwood lumber to the U.S. market. In parallel to our forceful representations to the Congress and Administration on this issue, our consultates in the U.S. have been alerting and mobilizing U.S. interests that would be adversely affected by the imposition of trade restrictions on Canadian lumber. Many of these U.S. interests, including the National Lumber and Building Materials Dealers Association, the Manufactured Housing Institute and the National Association of Home Builders are now actively lobbying against the proposed legislation. In addition our consultates have contacted the editorial boards of major newspapers across the U.S. to set the record straight and to ensure that they are aware of the facts. This activity has already shown positive results in terms of a number of editorials in U.S. publications, including the New York Times, supportive of the Canadian position.
The Government will continue to work closely with the Canadian industry in provinces to safeguard access for
October 8, 1985

Canadian softwood lumber products to the important U.S. market.
1 should like to refer to a statement made by U.S. Ambassador Niles last week suggesting that the Canadian lumber industry might help to take some of the heat out of protectionist pressures in the U.S. to restrict imports of Canadian softwood lumber by voluntarily restraining its export levels to the U.S. market. My understanding is that this was a personal view expressed by the U.S. ambassador. Any such action might well have serious anti-trust implications and these are considerations which would, I am certain, be taken fully into account by the Canadian industry. I want to underline that, for its part, the Canadian Government has not been asked to negotiate a restraint arrangement nor is it prepared at this time to entertain such a possibility.
Canada stands to suffer more than any other foreign country if the U.S. Congress imposes new restrictions on imports. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is well aware of that, and that is precisely why he wrote the President of the United States with a view to exploring with the Congress-

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to follow up on a question I directed to the Hon. Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) concerning a national historical project that has been identified for an area of Guysborough County in my constituency. I prefaced my question to the Minister by indicating the very severe economic circumstances in which we find ourselves in that part of Canada and I also highlighted the commitment of the Government of Canada to getting the economic show on the road in this region. Last week I identified for the Government a series of initiatives and this was one of them.
Grassy Island National Historic Site has been studied by officials of Parks Canada and a very thorough management plan has been prepared which reviews in some detail the benefits of this project. In addition to its historical significance, it has very important economic benefits in that it opens up an area of Guysborough County to the tourism industry.
Canso is a community that is at the end of a highway on a piece of land that juts out into the ocean and, for that obvious reason, it became one of our early fishing fortresses. However, today that represents a difficulty when it comes to developing the tourism industry.
This project is seen as an important catalyst to drawing tourists along the eastern shore of Nova Scotia and into the Canso area so that those in the area can develop restaurants and motel facilities and diversity the local economy, which to this point is almost totally dependent upon the fishing indus-
Adjournment Debate
try, an industry which has served Nova Scotia so well for several centuries.
The historical significance of the area is also well known to the people there. The people have embraced this project as a reflection of their identity, as a project through which they can express the great pride they have in their history and as a showcase for all Canadians. It is the site of the first fishing fortress in North America and in that respect has national significance for all Canadians. My constituents have very aggressively promoted this project for a number of decades.
I was very pleased to hear from the Minister yesterday that he as well embraces this project and has made it a personal priority. The Minister and I had the opportunity on another occasion to discuss in some detail the economic, social and historical benefits that this project will bring to my constituents. My constituents are prepared to build on their strengths, to become self-sufficient, to offer their resources and to build the jobs that we require. We are now looking to the Government to do its part in bringing forward this important initiative which is really not a costly project in the total picture. I look forward to hearing the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister in following up this matter in order that this project can get off the ground at an early date.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to start by thanking the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) for his ongoing excellent representation in the interests of seeing the Grassy Island park come to fruition. He has described very well not only the principal factor which has attracted the federal Government to this area, but also the important local aspects in terms of the economy should we see this area proclaimed, if you will, a national historic site as soon as possible.
There are several matters which we would like to emphasize with respect to the historic aspects. While it has been indicated that this is perhaps the first fishing fortress in North America, since the 17th and 18th centuries it has been the starting point when looking back to see where our fishing industry began. It gives us an opportunity to identify that for Canadians in a number of interesting ways.
I wish to spend the next few moments talking about the items we have planned for the future, as a part of the 1983 management plan development Parks Canada, to give people an indication of what we have in store. Having already spent a major portion of the total $1.7 million allocated, we are looking forward in the near future to the construction of a visitors reception centre, the preservation and stabilization of the heritage resources, including the foundations of various domestic and commercial buildings and the earthen walls of For William Augustus, and the interpretation of Grassy Island's historical resources, both in the visitor reception centre and on the island. Artifacts recovered from the late 1970 achaeological investigations on the island will be used in the visitors centre. A boat access from the mainland to the

October 8, 1985
Adjournment Debate
island, including dock facilities near the visitors centre and the island, will be provided. Last, but not least, washroom and parking facilities will be provided.
These proposals add up to an exciting development package for this area. With the continued efforts of the Hon. Member who has, in fact, discussed this matter with the Minister and with departmental officials, I know we will see things unfold in this area in the reasonably near future.
The constraints we have are really two. It is clear that we are in a tight spot financially and that there is a budgetary problem with which the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has to deal in regard to capital expenditures. There is a significant effort required for the engineering and additional planning for many of these facilities. However, with the indication the Hon. Member has already received from the Minister I think he can count on this being done in the reasonably near future.
